chapters.abstract: This section provides a brief bibliography of prominent textbooks and reference works in artificial intelligence and related fields, listing titles, editions, and authors. It serves as a quick reference for students to identify key resources covering topics such as AI fundamentals, computer vision, natural language processing, and probabilistic modeling. | Key concepts: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning, Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing (NLP), Bayesian Networks, Common Lisp, AI Textbooks, Reference Editions | Example questions: What are the major textbook references for studying artificial intelligence and its sub‑fields?; Which books should I consult for learning about Bayesian networks and computer vision?

chapters.title: Title Page
chapters.abstract: This section presents the title page of the textbook, listing the full title, edition, primary authors, contributing writers, and the various cities associated with its publication. It serves as the bibliographic front matter that identifies the work and its creators. | Key concepts: Title page, Edition, Primary authors, Contributing writers, Publication locations, Bibliographic information, Third Edition | Example questions: Who are the main authors and contributors of the textbook?; Which edition of 'Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach' is shown on the title page?

chapters.title: Copyright
chapters.abstract: This section presents the title‑page information for the textbook, listing the editorial and production staff, crediting image sources, and providing the copyright notice along with legal statements about usage rights, permissions, and liability. It outlines the publisher’s claim to all rights and the disclaimer that the author and publisher give no warranty for the content. | Key concepts: Copyright notice, All rights reserved, Permissions request process, Prohibited reproduction (electronic, mechanical, photocopying, etc.), Liability disclaimer, Editorial and production staff roles, Image source attribution, Publication manufacturing location | Example questions: Who do I contact to get permission to reproduce material from this textbook?; What legal restrictions does the copyright notice place on copying or distributing the book’s content?

chapters.title: Contents
chapters.abstract: This section outlines the textbook’s structure, detailing the progression from an introduction to artificial intelligence through the fundamentals of intelligent agents, and then into various problem‑solving techniques such as search strategies, heuristics, and online/partial‑observation methods. It serves as a roadmap of the topics and sub‑topics covered in each chapter, including summaries, bibliographic notes, and exercises. | Key concepts: Artificial Intelligence, Intelligent Agents, Rationality, Search Strategies (uninformed & informed), Heuristic Functions, Local Search, Nondeterministic Actions, Partial Observations, Online Search Agents, Problem‑Solving Agents | Example questions: What different search strategies does the textbook discuss for solving AI problems?; How does the book define rational behavior for intelligent agents and what environments are considered?

chapters.title: I: Artificial Intelligence
chapters.abstract: This section introduces artificial intelligence, explaining why it is a compelling field of study, outlining its historical origins, and presenting multiple definitions that contrast thought‑process versus behavior and human‑like versus rational performance criteria. | Key concepts: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Intelligence, Rationality, Human‑like performance, Behavior‑based definition, Thought‑process definition, AI subfields (learning, perception, etc.), Historical milestone (1956 Dartmouth conference), Universal applicability of AI | Example questions: What are the main ways AI is defined and how do they differ in terms of focusing on thought processes versus observable behavior?; Why is AI considered a field with many open research opportunities compared to more established sciences like physics?

children.title: 1 Introduction
children.abstract: This introductory section explains why artificial intelligence (AI) is a compelling field of study and outlines its historical origins, scope, and ambition to both understand and construct intelligent systems. It also presents a framework of AI definitions, contrasting thought‑process versus behavior approaches and human‑like versus rational performance criteria. | Key concepts: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Intelligence, Rationality, Human-like performance, Ideal performance measure, Subfields of AI (learning, perception, game playing, theorem proving, etc.), Historical origin (1956 naming), AI definitions matrix | Example questions: What are the main ways researchers define artificial intelligence and how do they differ?; Why is AI considered a promising field for new breakthroughs compared to older sciences like physics?

children.title: 1.1 What Is AI?
children.abstract: This section introduces artificial intelligence (AI) as a discipline, outlining its historical origins, its ambition to both understand and construct intelligent systems, and its breadth across many sub‑fields. It also presents a framework of eight AI definitions that vary along the axes of thought vs. behavior and human‑like performance vs. rational optimality. | Key concepts: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Intelligence, Rationality, Human‑level performance, Ideal performance measure, Subfields of AI (learning, perception, game playing, theorem proving, etc.), Historical origin (1956 naming, post‑WWII development), Definition dimensions (thought vs. behavior, human fidelity vs. rationality) | Example questions: What are the main ways researchers define AI and how do those definitions differ?; Why is AI considered a field with many open research opportunities compared to older sciences like physics?

children.title: 1.2 The Foundations of Artificial Intelligence
children.abstract: Section 1.2 introduces the foundational ideas of artificial intelligence, focusing on the notion of rational agents, the distinction between perfect and limited rationality, and a brief historical overview of the disciplines that shaped AI. It emphasizes why rationality is a useful analytical starting point despite computational constraints. | Key concepts: Rational agent, Perfect rationality, Limited rationality, Computational feasibility, AI history, Philosophical foundations of AI, Human behavior vs. rational models, General principles of AI, Agent design | Example questions: What is the difference between perfect rationality and limited rationality in AI?; Why do AI textbooks focus on rational agents rather than directly modeling human behavior?

children.title: 1.3 The History of Artificial Intelligence
children.abstract: This section outlines the early intellectual roots of artificial intelligence, highlighting the shift from behaviorist psychology to Chomsky's generative linguistics and the emergence of computational linguistics/NLP. It then traces the first formal AI work (1943‑1955) by McCulloch and Pitts, who combined neuroscience insights with formal logic. | Key concepts: Behaviorism, Noam Chomsky, Syntactic Structures, Computational Linguistics, Natural Language Processing (NLP), Knowledge Representation, Warren McCulloch, Walter Pitts, Propositional Logic, Russell and Whitehead | Example questions: How did Chomsky's critique of behaviorism influence the development of AI and computational linguistics?; What were the main contributions of McCulloch and Pitts to the early history of artificial intelligence?

children.title: 1.4 The State of the Art
children.abstract: The section discusses how the availability of massive data sets dramatically improves AI performance, often outweighing algorithmic differences, and illustrates this with examples from natural‑language processing and image completion. It also highlights the shift from hand‑coded knowledge engineering toward data‑driven learning, noting the emergence of many practical AI applications such as driverless vehicles. | Key concepts: Knowledge bottleneck, Data‑driven learning, Banko & Brill (2001) – scaling data in NLP, Hays & Efros (2007) – image completion with large photo collections, AI Spring vs. AI Winter, DARPA Grand Challenge, Stanley (driverless robotic car), Halevy et al. (2009) – learning over hand‑coded knowledge, Kurzweil (2005) – AI embedded in industry | Example questions: Why does increasing the amount of training data often improve AI performance more than changing the algorithm?; What are some real‑world examples that show the impact of large data sets on AI capabilities?

children.title: 1.5 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes several real‑world AI applications highlighted in the chapter, including IBM’s Deep Blue chess system, machine‑learning spam filters, the DART logistics‑planning tool used in the Gulf War, and commercial/military robotics such as iRobot’s Roomba and PackBot. It also points to the bibliographic references and exercises that follow. | Key concepts: Deep Blue, Garry Kasparov, Spam filtering / learning algorithms, Dynamic Analysis and Replanning Tool (DART), DARPA’s AI investment, AI planning, iRobot Roomba, PackBot, Artificial Intelligence applications | Example questions: What are some notable examples of AI systems that have had a major impact in fields like games, email, logistics, and robotics?; How did the DART system demonstrate the practical value of AI planning during the 1991 Persian Gulf crisis?

children.title: 2 Intelligent Agents
children.abstract: This section introduces the foundational idea of intelligent agents, defining them as entities that perceive their environment through sensors and act via actuators. It explains rational agents, how environment characteristics affect agent design, and presents basic agent architectures. | Key concepts: Agent, Environment, Sensor, Actuator, Percept, Percept sequence, Rational agent, Environment properties (e.g., observability, determinism), Agent design skeletons | Example questions: What is the difference between a sensor and an actuator in the context of an intelligent agent?; How does the notion of a rational agent depend on the characteristics of its environment?

children.title: 2.1 Agents and Environments
children.abstract: Section 2.1 introduces the fundamental notion of an agent as an entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon it via actuators. It explains how the interaction between agents and environments gives rise to the concept of rational agents, and outlines a basic taxonomy of environments that influences agent design. | Key concepts: Agent, Environment, Sensor, Actuator, Percept, Percept sequence, Rational agent, Environment categorization (e.g., deterministic vs stochastic, fully vs partially observable), Agent design skeletons | Example questions: What defines an agent in the context of artificial intelligence and how does it interact with its environment?; How does the nature of an environment affect the design of a rational agent?

children.title: 2.2 Good Behavior: The Concept of Rationality
children.abstract: This section introduces the notion of rationality for intelligent agents, defining a rational agent as one that selects actions that maximize a performance measure based on its percept history. It emphasizes that rational behavior is judged by the desirability of the resulting state sequences in the environment, not merely by the internal structure of the agent. | Key concepts: Intelligent agent, Agent function, Percept sequence, Rational agent, Performance measure, Vacuum‑cleaner world example, Desirability of state sequences, Decision making in AI | Example questions: What does it mean for an agent to be rational according to the textbook?; How is a performance measure used to evaluate the behavior of an intelligent agent?

children.title: 2.3 The Nature of Environments
children.abstract: This section introduces the concept of a task environment for rational agents, explaining how to fully specify it using the PEAS (Performance measure, Environment, Actuators, Sensors) framework. It illustrates the process with examples, notably a vacuum‑cleaner agent and a more complex automated taxi driver, and discusses how the nature of the environment influences agent design. | Key concepts: Task environment, Rational agent, PEAS description, Performance measure, Actuators, Sensors, Environment characteristics, Open‑ended tasks, Agent design implications | Example questions: How do I use the PEAS framework to define the task environment for a new AI agent?; Why does the nature of the task environment affect the design of an agent’s program?

children.title: 2.4 The Structure of Agents
children.abstract: Section 2.4 explains how an intelligent agent is built by separating the agent program—the software that maps percepts to actions—from the underlying hardware architecture that provides sensors and actuators. It emphasizes that the program must be compatible with the architecture and introduces the notion of a rational agent that maximizes expected performance over a class of environments. | Key concepts: Agent, Agent program, Architecture, Percept, Action, Sensors, Actuators, Rational agent, Environment class, Environment generator | Example questions: What is the difference between an agent's program and its architecture?; How does a rational agent maximize performance across an environment class?

children.title: 2.5 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes the core ideas of the chapter on artificial intelligence, framing AI as the science of designing agents that perceive and act in environments. It reviews the definitions of agents, performance measures, task‑environment specifications, the dimensions that characterize environments, various agent‑program architectures, and the role of learning in improving agent performance. | Key concepts: Agent function, Performance measure, Task environment specification, Observability (fully vs. partially observable), Deterministic vs. stochastic environments, Simple reflex agent, Model‑based reflex agent, Goal‑based agent, Utility‑based agent, Learning | Example questions: What are the main dimensions used to classify task environments in AI?; How do goal‑based agents differ from utility‑based agents in their decision‑making process?

chapters.title: II: Problem-solving
chapters.abstract: This section introduces problem‑solving agents that search for a sequence of actions to achieve a goal, contrasting them with simple reflex agents. It defines problems and solutions, explains atomic state representations, and surveys uninformed and informed search algorithms, touching on their computational complexity and NP‑completeness. | Key concepts: Problem‑solving agent, Atomic state representation, Goal‑based agent, Uninformed (blind) search, Informed (heuristic) search, Search algorithm, Asymptotic complexity (O‑notation), NP‑completeness, Fixed action sequence | Example questions: How do problem‑solving agents differ from reflex agents, and what role does search play in their operation?; What is the difference between uninformed and informed search algorithms, and why does complexity matter for solving problems?

children.title: 3 Solving Problems by Searching
children.abstract: This section introduces problem‑solving agents that search for a sequence of actions to achieve a goal, contrasting them with reflex agents and outlining the distinction between atomic (unstructured) representations and more complex planning representations. It then defines problems and solutions and previews uninformed and informed search algorithms, discussing their efficiency and the role of asymptotic complexity and NP‑completeness. | Key concepts: Problem‑solving agent, Atomic representation, Goal‑based agent, Uninformed search algorithm, Informed search algorithm, Asymptotic complexity (O‑notation), NP‑completeness, Search space, State‑action mapping, Planning agent | Example questions: How do problem‑solving agents differ from reflex agents, and what role does search play in their operation?; What is the difference between uninformed and informed search algorithms, and why are they important for solving problems efficiently?

children.title: 3.1 Problem-Solving Agents
children.abstract: This section introduces problem‑solving agents, a type of goal‑based agent that searches for a fixed sequence of actions to achieve its goals. It defines problems and solutions, distinguishes atomic (unstructured) state representations from factored ones, and outlines both uninformed and informed search strategies used to find solutions. | Key concepts: Problem‑solving agent, Atomic (unstructured) state representation, Goal‑based agent, Uninformed (blind) search algorithms, Informed (heuristic) search algorithms, Search space, Solution path, Asymptotic complexity (O‑notation), NP‑completeness | Example questions: What is a problem‑solving agent and how does it differ from a reflex or planning agent?; How do uninformed and informed search algorithms differ in their use for solving problems?

children.title: 3.2 Example Problems
children.abstract: This section explains the role of abstraction in problem‑solving, showing how both state descriptions and actions are simplified by omitting irrelevant details, and discusses how an abstract solution must be expandable into a concrete solution in the detailed world. | Key concepts: Abstraction, State description, Action abstraction, Abstract solution, Detailed world/state, Representation, State space, Solution expansion, Validity condition for abstraction | Example questions: Why do we need to abstract states and actions when modeling a route‑finding problem?; What does it mean for an abstract solution to be valid, and how can we verify that it can be expanded into a concrete solution?

children.title: 3.3 Searching for Solutions
children.abstract: This section introduces the fundamentals of search‑based problem solving, describing how possible action sequences form a search tree rooted at the initial state, how nodes are expanded by applying legal actions, and why practical algorithms must prune the vast state space. It uses the classic route‑finding example (Arad to Bucharest) to illustrate concepts such as expansion, parent/child nodes, and the need to manage alternative paths. | Key concepts: Search tree, Node (state), Root node, Parent node, Child node, Expansion (generating successors), Legal actions, State space, Goal test, Pruning / search space reduction | Example questions: How does a search tree represent the set of possible action sequences in a problem‑solving task?; What does it mean to expand a node in a search tree, and why is pruning necessary for large state spaces?

children.title: 3.4 Uninformed Search Strategies
children.abstract: This section introduces uninformed (or blind) search strategies, which explore the state space without any heuristic guidance, and explains how they differ from informed (heuristic) searches. It details breadth‑first search as a primary example, describing its operation using a FIFO queue to always expand the shallowest unexpanded node. | Key concepts: Uninformed search (blind search), Informed search (heuristic search), Breadth‑first search (BFS), FIFO queue, Frontier, Graph‑search algorithm, Shallowest unexpanded node, Depth (level) of a node, Goal test | Example questions: What is the main difference between uninformed (blind) search and informed (heuristic) search?; How does breadth‑first search ensure that it expands nodes in order of increasing depth?

children.title: 3.5 Informed (Heuristic) Search Strategies
children.abstract: This section introduces informed (heuristic) search strategies, focusing on best‑first search where nodes are selected for expansion using an evaluation function f(n) that incorporates a heuristic estimate h(n). It explains how the choice of f determines the search behavior and outlines greedy best‑first search as a specific instance that expands the node estimated to be closest to the goal. | Key concepts: Best‑first search, Evaluation function f(n), Heuristic function h(n), Uniform‑cost search, Greedy best‑first search, Priority queue ordering, Tree‑search vs. graph‑search, Admissible heuristic (mentioned later), Problem‑specific knowledge | Example questions: How does a heuristic function influence the order in which nodes are expanded in best‑first search?; What is the difference between greedy best‑first search and uniform‑cost search?

children.title: 3.6 Heuristic Functions
children.abstract: Section 3.6 explains how heuristic functions guide informed search algorithms, defining their required properties (admissibility, consistency) and showing how good heuristics improve efficiency and guarantee optimality. It also covers techniques for constructing and combining heuristics, such as dominance, weighted A*, and pattern‑database methods. | Key concepts: Heuristic function h(n), Evaluation function f(n) = g(n) + h(n), Admissible heuristic, Consistent (monotonic) heuristic, Heuristic dominance, Weighted A*, Pattern database heuristic, Informed (best‑first) search, Heuristic design techniques | Example questions: What does it mean for a heuristic to be admissible, and why is that property important for A*?; How does heuristic consistency ensure that A* expands nodes in optimal order?

children.title: 3.7 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: Section 3.7 summarizes the fundamentals of search‑based problem solving in deterministic, fully observable environments. It reviews how a problem is formally defined, the distinction between tree‑search and graph‑search, and the key properties and trade‑offs of uninformed search algorithms such as breadth‑first, uniform‑cost, depth‑first, depth‑limited, and iterative‑deepening search. | Key concepts: Problem formulation (initial state, actions, transition model, goal test, path cost), State space, Tree‑search vs. Graph‑search, Completeness, Optimality, Time complexity (branching factor b, solution depth d), Space complexity, Breadth‑first search, Uniform‑cost search, Iterative deepening search | Example questions: What are the main differences between tree‑search and graph‑search, and why does graph‑search avoid redundant paths?; Which uninformed search algorithm is both complete and optimal for unit step costs, and what are its time and space complexities?

children.title: 4 Beyond Classical Search
children.abstract: This section introduces search methods that go beyond the classical assumptions of fully observable, deterministic, and known environments. It covers local‑search techniques such as hill climbing, simulated annealing, and genetic algorithms, and explains how they address optimization problems where only the final state matters, not the path taken. | Key concepts: Local search, Hill climbing, Simulated annealing, Genetic algorithms, Optimization problem, State space, Partial observability, Determinism, Online search | Example questions: What are the main differences between systematic search and local‑search algorithms?; How does simulated annealing help avoid getting stuck in local optima during optimization?

children.title: 4.1 Local Search Algorithms and Optimization Problems
children.abstract: Section 4.1 introduces local‑search methods for solving optimization problems, emphasizing that only the final state matters, not the path taken to reach it. It explains how these algorithms explore the neighborhood of a current state, using evaluation functions to guide moves, and discusses common issues such as local optima, plateaus, and strategies like random restarts. | Key concepts: Local search, Optimization problem, Evaluation (objective) function, Neighbourhood structure, Hill climbing, Local optimum, Plateau, Random restart, Simulated annealing (as a later extension), Genetic algorithm (as a later extension) | Example questions: How do local‑search algorithms differ from systematic search methods, and why are they suitable for problems like the 8‑queens?; What techniques can be used to avoid getting stuck in local optima when applying hill‑climbing search?

children.title: 4.2 Local Search in Continuous Spaces
children.abstract: This section introduces local search techniques for continuous problem spaces, focusing on genetic algorithms as a population‑based method that uses selection, crossover, and mutation to evolve solutions. It discusses the importance of representation, practical applications, and the challenges of applying local search in environments with infinite branching factors. | Key concepts: Genetic Algorithm, Fitness Function, Selection (Random Selection based on fitness), Crossover / Reproduce, Mutation, Representation of individuals, Continuous vs. Discrete search spaces, Branching factor, Hill climbing, Simulated annealing | Example questions: How does a genetic algorithm perform local search in a continuous space, and what are its main operators?; Why are traditional hill climbing and simulated annealing better suited than simple local search for continuous environments?

children.title: 4.3 Searching with Nondeterministic Actions
children.abstract: This section introduces search problems where actions can have multiple possible outcomes (nondeterministic) or where the agent cannot fully observe the current state. It explains how percepts become essential for narrowing down possible states and outlines the concepts and methods (e.g., belief states, AND‑OR graphs) used to plan under such uncertainty. | Key concepts: Nondeterministic actions, Partially observable environment, Percept, Belief state (set of possible states), AND‑OR graph, Contingency planning, Solution policy, Deterministic vs. nondeterministic search, State space | Example questions: How does a search algorithm handle actions that can lead to multiple possible successor states?; What role do percepts play in partially observable or nondeterministic environments?

children.title: 4.4 Searching with Partial Observations
children.abstract: Section 4.4 introduces the challenge of partial observability in search problems, explaining how an agent’s limited percepts lead to uncertainty about its true state. It defines the belief state as a representation of all possible world states consistent with the agent’s action‑percept history, and examines the simplest case—sensorless (conformant) problems—before extending to partial sensing and nondeterministic actions. | Key concepts: Partial observability, Belief state, Sensorless (conformant) problem, Conformant planning, Partial sensing, Deterministic vs nondeterministic actions, Observable vs unobservable properties, Action outcome uncertainty | Example questions: How does a belief state help an agent plan when its sensors provide incomplete information?; What is a sensorless (conformant) problem and why can it still be solvable without any observations?

children.title: 4.5 Online Search Agents and Unknown Environments
children.abstract: This section contrasts offline and online search agents, explaining how online search interleaves computation with action to handle dynamic, nondeterministic, or unknown environments. It introduces the exploration problem, where an agent must learn about the state space through its actions, using examples such as a robot mapping a new building or a newborn learning about the world. | Key concepts: Online search, Offline search, Dynamic domain, Nondeterministic domain, Unknown environment, Exploration problem, Interleaved computation and action, Map building (spatial exploration), Planning horizon trade‑off, Contingency handling | Example questions: Why is online search preferred over offline search in a robot that must navigate an unfamiliar building?; How does the exploration problem relate to an agent operating in an unknown or nondeterministic environment?

children.title: 4.6 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: Section 4.6 reviews the learning capabilities of online search agents, describing how they can acquire a map of deterministic environments and improve state‑cost estimates through local updating rules such as LRTA*. It also highlights the need for explicit representations of action effects and algorithms that can generalize these learned rules. | Key concepts: Online search agents, LRTA* (Learning Real‑Time A*), Deterministic environment, Result function, State‑cost estimation, Local updating rules, Hill climbing optimality, Map learning, General action rules | Example questions: How do online search agents learn the layout of a deterministic environment and improve their cost estimates?; Why is an explicit representation of action effects needed beyond the RESULT function in online search?

children.title: 5 Adversarial Search
children.abstract: This section introduces adversarial search, focusing on competitive two‑player games that are deterministic, turn‑taking, zero‑sum, and have perfect information. It explains how such games are modeled in AI and why they are useful testbeds for search algorithms. | Key concepts: Adversarial search, Zero‑sum game, Perfect information, Deterministic environment, Turn‑taking, Multi‑agent environment, Game state representation, Utility (payoff) function, Competitive vs. cooperative agents | Example questions: What characteristics define the type of games typically studied in adversarial search?; How does a zero‑sum game differ from other multi‑agent scenarios in terms of utility values?

children.title: 5.1 Games
children.abstract: This section introduces adversarial search by defining games as deterministic, turn‑taking, two‑player zero‑sum environments with perfect information. It explains why such games are useful models for AI research and contrasts them with more complex physical games. | Key concepts: Adversarial search, Zero‑sum game, Perfect information, Deterministic game, Turn‑taking, Multi‑agent environment, Utility function, Game state representation, Game theory | Example questions: What characteristics define a zero‑sum game with perfect information?; Why are deterministic turn‑taking games like chess useful for studying adversarial search in AI?

children.title: 5.2 Optimal Decisions in Games
children.abstract: This section introduces adversarial (game) search, explaining how MAX and MIN construct a search tree over the game’s possible moves, assign utility values to terminal states, and use strategies like minimax to choose optimal actions. It contrasts the size of game trees in simple games like tic‑tac‑toe with complex ones like chess and defines the concept of a contingent strategy for the maximizing player. | Key concepts: Game tree, Search tree, MAX and MIN players, Utility value, Terminal state, Contingent strategy, Minimax algorithm, Two‑ply tree, Adversarial search | Example questions: How does the minimax algorithm determine the best move for MAX in a game tree?; What is a contingent strategy and why is it needed in adversarial search?

children.title: 5.3 Alpha–Beta Pruning
children.abstract: This section introduces alpha–beta pruning, a technique that speeds up minimax search by eliminating branches of the game tree that cannot affect the final decision. It explains how the algorithm maintains alpha (the best already‑found option for the maximizer) and beta (the best already‑found option for the minimizer) bounds and prunes nodes when these bounds cross, achieving the same optimal move as full minimax with far fewer node evaluations. | Key concepts: Minimax search, Game tree, Exponential growth of nodes, Alpha (α) value, Beta (β) value, Alpha–beta pruning, Branch pruning condition (α ≥ β), Search depth / ply, Optimal move | Example questions: How does alpha–beta pruning reduce the number of nodes examined compared to plain minimax?; What are the roles of the alpha and beta values in deciding when to prune a branch?

children.title: 5.4 Imperfect Real-Time Decisions
children.abstract: This section explains how real‑time game‑playing programs handle the impossibility of searching to terminal states by introducing heuristic evaluation functions and cutoff tests, turning deep non‑terminal nodes into leaf nodes. It also discusses practical concerns such as using transposition tables and pruning techniques (alpha‑beta) to manage the search space within time constraints. | Key concepts: Heuristic minimax (H‑MINIMAX), Evaluation function (EVAL), Cutoff test, Alpha‑beta pruning, Transposition table, Search depth limit, Utility function, MAX and MIN players, Terminal test | Example questions: How do heuristic evaluation functions and cutoff tests allow a game‑playing program to make decisions without searching to terminal states?; What strategies can be used to limit the size of a transposition table when evaluating millions of nodes per second?

children.title: 5.5 Stochastic Games
children.abstract: This section introduces stochastic games—games that combine chance and skill—using backgammon as a primary example. It explains how game trees for such games must incorporate chance nodes that represent random events (like dice rolls) and discusses the calculation of roll probabilities. | Key concepts: Stochastic game, Chance node, Game tree, MAX node, MIN node, Dice roll probability, Distinct roll, Doubles (e.g., 1‑1, 2‑2), Backgammon | Example questions: How do chance nodes differ from MAX and MIN nodes in a game tree for backgammon?; What is the probability of rolling a specific non‑double (e.g., 5‑3) in a two‑dice stochastic game?

children.title: 5.6 Partially Observable Games
children.abstract: This section explains how adversarial search techniques can be extended to games that include chance events and partial observability. It covers pruning chance nodes by using utility bounds, the use of Monte Carlo simulations (rollouts) to estimate position values, and the role of fog‑of‑war concepts such as scouts and spies in partially observable games. | Key concepts: Chance node, Alpha‑beta pruning, Utility bounds, Monte Carlo simulation, Rollout, Partial observability, Fog of war, Scouts and spies, Expected value, Adversarial search | Example questions: How can alpha‑beta pruning be applied to chance nodes in a game tree?; What is a rollout and how does Monte Carlo simulation help evaluate positions in partially observable games?

children.title: 5.7 State-of-the-Art Game Programs
children.abstract: This section examines the characteristics of cutting‑edge game programs, using IBM’s Deep Blue chess system as a case study. It explains how specialized hardware, massive parallelism, sophisticated search techniques, and extensive opening/endgame knowledge combine to achieve world‑class performance. | Key concepts: Alpha–beta search, VLSI chess processors, Singular extensions, Opening book, Endgame database, Evaluation function (8000+ features), Parallel computing (IBM RS/6000 processors), Move generation and ordering, Forced/forcing moves | Example questions: How did Deep Blue’s hardware architecture contribute to its ability to search billions of positions per move?; What search techniques did Deep Blue use to go beyond the normal depth limit in chess positions?

children.title: 5.8 Alternative Approaches
children.abstract: This section discusses alternative AI approaches for solving partially observable games such as bridge, highlighting the use of hierarchical planning, Monte‑Carlo simulation, and explanation‑based generalization in programs like Bridge Baron and GIB. It explains how these techniques enable efficient reasoning about large decision spaces and improve tactical performance despite limited information gathering capabilities. | Key concepts: Monte Carlo simulation, Explanation‑Based Generalization (EBG), Hierarchical planning, Partially observable games, Bridge Baron, GIB (Ginsberg’s Bridge program), Information gathering, Tactical accuracy, Cache of general rules, High‑level bridge concepts (e.g., finesse, squeeze) | Example questions: How does the GIB program use explanation‑based generalization to reduce the number of situations it must evaluate?; Why are Monte‑Carlo methods more successful for bridge AI than for Kriegspiel programs?

children.title: 5.9 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section introduces the concept of metareasoning in game‑tree search, emphasizing the utility of node expansions and when a search algorithm should stop expanding nodes. It contrasts traditional heuristic search with goal‑directed planning and hints at more advanced metareasoning techniques discussed later in the book. | Key concepts: Metareasoning, Utility of node expansion, Alpha–beta pruning, Search cost vs. benefit trade‑off, Goal‑directed reasoning / planning, Symmetrical move handling, Heuristic evaluation function, PARADISE program, Stopping criteria for search | Example questions: When should a game‑playing algorithm stop expanding nodes and make a move according to the utility concept?; How does metareasoning differ from the basic alpha‑beta pruning technique described in this section?

children.title: 6 Constraint Satisfaction Problems
children.abstract: This section introduces Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) as a factored way to represent states using variables, domains, and constraints. It explains the three core components of a CSP (variables X, domains D, constraints C) and how CSP‑specific search algorithms exploit this structure to prune large parts of the search space. | Key concepts: Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP), Variable, Domain, Constraint, Scope (of a constraint), Relation (allowed tuples), Factored state representation, CSP search algorithm, General‑purpose heuristics, Black‑box state model | Example questions: What are the three components that define a constraint satisfaction problem?; How does representing a problem with variables and domains help CSP search algorithms eliminate large portions of the search space?

children.title: 6.1 Defining Constraint Satisfaction Problems
children.abstract: This section introduces Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs) as a factored way to represent states using variables, domains, and constraints. It defines the three core components of a CSP (variables X, domains D, and constraints C) and explains how constraints are expressed as scopes and relations, laying the groundwork for CSP‑specific search techniques. | Key concepts: Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP), Variable (X_i), Domain (D_i), Constraint (C_i), Scope, Relation (rel), Factored state representation, Search space pruning, Explicit tuple representation | Example questions: What are the three fundamental components that define a constraint satisfaction problem?; How does a constraint’s scope and relation specify the allowed combinations of variable values in a CSP?

children.title: 6.2 Constraint Propagation: Inference in CSPs
children.abstract: This section introduces constraint propagation as an inference technique for solving Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSPs). It explains how local consistency—starting with node consistency and extending to other forms—can prune variable domains before or during search, sometimes solving the problem outright. | Key concepts: Constraint propagation, Local consistency, Node consistency, Unary constraints, Binary constraints, Domain reduction, CSP network graph, Preprocessing vs. interleaved inference, Arc consistency (previewed later), Search vs. inference trade‑off | Example questions: How does node consistency help reduce the domains of variables in a CSP?; What is the difference between using constraint propagation as a preprocessing step and interleaving it with search?

children.title: 6.3 Backtracking Search for CSPs
children.abstract: This section introduces backtracking search as a fundamental algorithm for solving constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) when inference techniques like arc‑consistency are insufficient. It explains how systematic variable assignment, recursive depth‑first search, and pruning via consistency checks can efficiently explore the solution space. | Key concepts: Backtracking search, Depth‑first search, Variable ordering heuristics, Value ordering heuristics, Constraint propagation, Forward checking, Arc consistency (AC‑3), Domain pruning, Search tree | Example questions: How does backtracking search work for solving CSPs and why is it needed beyond inference methods?; What heuristics can be used to improve the efficiency of backtracking search in a CSP?

children.title: 6.4 Local Search for CSPs
children.abstract: This section explains how backjumping improves depth‑first search for CSPs by using conflict sets to jump directly to the most recent variable responsible for a dead‑end, and introduces constraint learning (recording no‑goods) to prevent revisiting the same failing combinations. It shows how these techniques work together to prune the search space more efficiently than plain backtracking. | Key concepts: Backjumping, Conflict set, Constraint learning, No‑good, Forward checking, Backtracking, Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP), Variable ordering | Example questions: How does backjumping decide which variable to backtrack to when a conflict occurs?; What is a no‑good in constraint learning, and how does recording it help the search?

children.title: 6.5 The Structure of Problems
children.abstract: Section 6.5 discusses how to structure constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs) for effective solving, focusing on local‑search strategies such as min‑conflicts, plateau search, tabu search, simulated annealing, and constraint weighting. It also highlights the adaptability of local search for online and dynamic scheduling scenarios. | Key concepts: Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP), Min‑conflicts heuristic, Plateau search, Tabu search, Simulated annealing, Constraint weighting, Local search, Online/dynamic problem solving, Backtracking search | Example questions: How does the constraint‑weighting technique improve local‑search performance on CSP plateaux?; What local‑search methods can be used to adapt a schedule when new constraints (e.g., weather disruptions) appear?

children.title: 6.6 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes the core concepts of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), covering how constraints are used for inference, the main search strategies (backtracking and local search), and the impact of the constraint‑graph structure on algorithmic efficiency. It also highlights key heuristics and structural techniques such as tree‑decomposition and cutset conditioning that make solving CSPs tractable. | Key concepts: Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP), Node/Arc/Path/k‑Consistency, Backtracking Search, Minimum‑Remaining‑Values (MRV) Heuristic, Degree Heuristic, Least‑Constraining‑Value Heuristic, Conflict‑Directed Backjumping, Local Search / Min‑Conflicts Heuristic, Tree‑Structured CSPs, Cutset Conditioning and Tree Decomposition | Example questions: What inference techniques (e.g., node, arc, path consistency) are used to prune variable/value pairs in a CSP?; How does the structure of a CSP’s constraint graph (such as being tree‑structured or having small tree width) influence the complexity of solving the problem?

chapters.title: III: Knowledge, reasoning, and planning
chapters.abstract: This section introduces logical (knowledge‑based) agents, explaining how they use internal representations and logical inference to reason about the world and decide actions. It contrasts these agents with earlier problem‑solving agents, highlighting the limitations of hard‑coded transition models and atomic state representations, and motivates the shift toward richer logical representations for flexible, domain‑independent reasoning. | Key concepts: Logical agents, Knowledge‑based agents, Representation, Reasoning / logical inference, Transition model, 8‑puzzle example, Partial observability, State variables (assignments), Domain‑independent algorithms, Logical formalism | Example questions: Why are problem‑solving agents considered limited compared to knowledge‑based agents?; How does using logical representations improve an agent’s ability to reason in partially observable environments?

children.title: 7 Logical Agents
children.abstract: This section introduces logical (knowledge‑based) agents, explaining how they use formal representations of knowledge and inference mechanisms to reason about the world and decide actions. It contrasts these agents with earlier problem‑solving agents, highlighting the limitations of hard‑coded transition models and atomic state representations, and motivates the shift to logical representations for more flexible, domain‑independent reasoning. | Key concepts: Logical agents, Knowledge‑based agents, Representation of knowledge, Inference / logical reasoning, Transition model, Partial observability, State variables (assignments), 8‑puzzle parity constraint, Domain‑independent reasoning | Example questions: Why are logical representations considered more flexible than the transition models used by problem‑solving agents?; How do knowledge‑based agents handle partially observable environments compared to earlier agents?

children.title: 7.1 Knowledge-Based Agents
children.abstract: Section 7.1 introduces knowledge‑based agents, focusing on the role of the knowledge base (KB) as the core component that stores logical sentences (axioms) expressed in a knowledge‑representation language. It explains the fundamental operations TELL (adding sentences) and ASK (querying the KB), and emphasizes that inference must be sound—answers must logically follow from the stored knowledge. | Key concepts: Knowledge Base (KB), Sentence (axiom), Knowledge Representation Language, TELL operation, ASK operation, Inference, Soundness of inference, Background knowledge, Propositional logic (as a KR language), Wumpus world example | Example questions: What are the main components and operations of a knowledge‑based agent?; How do the TELL and ASK functions interact with the knowledge base in a logical agent?

children.title: 7.2 The Wumpus World
children.abstract: This section introduces the architecture of logical (knowledge‑based) agents, illustrating how they update a knowledge base with percepts, query it for actions, and record taken actions. It also contrasts the knowledge level with the implementation level and explains the declarative versus procedural approaches to building such agents. | Key concepts: KB‑AGENT algorithm, Knowledge Base (KB), TELL and ASK operations, Knowledge level vs. implementation level, Declarative approach, Procedural approach, Percept sentence, Action query/sentence, Logical agents | Example questions: How does a knowledge‑based agent use TELL and ASK to choose its next action?; What is the difference between the declarative and procedural approaches to constructing an agent?

children.title: 7.3 Logic
children.abstract: Section 7.3 introduces the fundamentals of logical representation for intelligent agents, explaining how knowledge bases are built from well‑formed sentences, how syntax defines what counts as a valid sentence, and how semantics assigns truth values to those sentences in possible worlds (models). It emphasizes that logical inference yields guaranteed correct conclusions provided the underlying information is correct. | Key concepts: Logical agent, Knowledge base (KB), Syntax, Semantics, Truth value, Possible world, Model, Logical inference, Well‑formed sentence | Example questions: What is the difference between syntax and semantics in a logical representation?; How does a logical agent ensure that its conclusions are guaranteed to be correct?

children.title: 7.4 Propositional Logic: A Very Simple Logic
children.abstract: This section explains how propositional logic serves as a simple formalism for representing knowledge in an agent, linking logical sentences to real‑world aspects through grounding via sensors and learning. It discusses how a knowledge base’s truth is established by perceptual input and how general rules are acquired and may be fallible. | Key concepts: Propositional logic, Knowledge base (KB), Grounding, Sensors/percepts, Sentence construction, Logical entailment, General rules, Learning (rule acquisition), Wumpus‑world example | Example questions: How does an agent ensure that the sentences in its knowledge base correspond to actual facts in the environment?; What role do sensors and learning play in grounding propositional logic representations?

children.title: 7.5 Propositional Theorem Proving
children.abstract: This section introduces propositional theorem proving as an alternative to model‑checking for determining entailment. It explains logical equivalence, validity, and presents the standard logical equivalences that serve as inference rules for constructing proofs directly from a knowledge base. | Key concepts: Logical equivalence (α ≡ β), Entailment (α ⊨ β), Validity, Theorem proving, Standard logical equivalences (commutativity, associativity, De Morgan, distributivity, etc.), Implication elimination, Contraposition, Biconditional elimination, Double‑negation elimination | Example questions: How can I prove that a propositional sentence follows from a knowledge base without enumerating all models?; What are the standard logical equivalences used as inference rules in propositional theorem proving?

children.title: 7.6 Effective Propositional Model Checking
children.abstract: Section 7.6 introduces efficient propositional model‑checking techniques, contrasting forward‑chaining (data‑driven) and backward‑chaining (goal‑directed) inference on Horn‑clause knowledge bases, and then presents two families of general propositional algorithms—backtracking search and local hill‑climbing search—that operate in linear or near‑linear time. | Key concepts: Horn clauses, AND–OR graph, Forward chaining, Backward chaining, Goal‑directed reasoning, Linear‑time inference, Backtracking search, Hill‑climbing (local search), Propositional model checking | Example questions: How does backward chaining differ from forward chaining when answering a query in a Horn‑clause knowledge base?; What are the two main families of efficient propositional inference algorithms discussed in this section, and how do they work?

children.title: 7.7 Agents Based on Propositional Logic
children.abstract: Section 7.7 explains how to build a Wumpus‑world agent that uses propositional logic to infer the current state of the environment from its percept history. It covers constructing a complete logical model—including axioms about pits, the Wumpus, breezes, and stenches, as well as uniqueness constraints—and shows how the agent can maintain and update this knowledge efficiently for planning. | Key concepts: Knowledge base (KB), Propositional axioms, Breeze ↔ neighboring pit equivalence, Stench ↔ neighboring Wumpus equivalence, Exactly‑one constraint (uniqueness of the Wumpus), Logical inference for state estimation, Percept history integration, Planning via logical deduction | Example questions: How does a propositional‑logic agent represent the rule that a square is breezy iff an adjacent square contains a pit?; What logical sentences are used to enforce that there is exactly one Wumpus in the world?

children.title: 7.8 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes the role of knowledge in intelligent (logical) agents, explaining how knowledge bases and inference mechanisms enable decision‑making, and highlights the limitations of propositional logic that motivate the use of first‑order logic for compactly representing general rules about worlds like the Wumpus environment. | Key concepts: Knowledge‑based agent, Knowledge base, Inference mechanism, Representation language (syntax and semantics), Entailment, Propositional logic limitations, First‑order logic, Generalized sentence schemas, Logical reasoning | Example questions: Why can’t propositional logic efficiently represent rules that apply to every square and time step in a Wumpus world?; What are the main components of a knowledge‑based agent and how do they interact to decide on actions?

children.title: 8 First-Order Logic
children.abstract: This section introduces first‑order logic (FOL) as a more expressive representation language for knowledge‑based agents, contrasting it with propositional logic and discussing why richer languages are needed to model objects and their relationships. It outlines the role of representation languages, previews the syntax and semantics of FOL, and sets the stage for using FOL to capture commonsense knowledge. | Key concepts: First‑order logic (FOL), Propositional logic, Representation language, Syntax (of FOL), Semantics (of FOL), Predicates and arguments, Objects and relations, Knowledge‑based agents, Commonsense knowledge | Example questions: Why is propositional logic considered insufficient for representing complex environments in AI?; What are the basic syntactic and semantic components of first‑order logic?

children.title: 8.1 Representation Revisited
children.abstract: Section 8.1 revisits the purpose and requirements of representation languages for knowledge-based agents, contrasting the limitations of propositional logic with the expressive power needed for complex domains. It introduces first‑order logic as a more suitable formalism and briefly surveys other language families (e.g., programming languages) to motivate why richer representations are essential for commonsense reasoning. | Key concepts: Representation language, Propositional logic, First‑order logic (FOL), Expressiveness, Knowledge‑based agents, Formal semantics, Data structures as representations, Limitations of propositional representations, Commonsense knowledge | Example questions: Why is propositional logic considered insufficient for representing complex environments in AI?; What motivates the shift from propositional logic to first‑order logic in knowledge representation?

children.title: 8.2 Syntax and Semantics of First-Order Logic
children.abstract: Section 8.2 introduces the syntax and semantics of First‑Order Logic (FOL), explaining how its models represent possible worlds that contain objects and relations. It contrasts FOL’s ontological and epistemological commitments with those of other formal languages and outlines the basic elements of the language (constants, predicates, quantifiers, etc.) and how their meanings are defined. | Key concepts: First‑Order Logic (FOL), Ontological commitment, Epistemological commitment, Model (interpretation) for FOL, Vocabulary (constants, predicates, functions), Syntax (well‑formed formulas, quantifiers), Semantics (truth valuation in a model), Possible world, Relation, Object | Example questions: How does a first‑order logic model map the symbols of a sentence to objects and relations in a possible world?; What are the main syntactic components of first‑order logic and how are their meanings (semantics) defined?

children.title: 8.3 Using First-Order Logic
children.abstract: This section introduces *database semantics* for first‑order logic, contrasting it with the standard semantics by fixing the domain to exactly the objects named by constant symbols. It illustrates how the number of possible models is drastically reduced (e.g., 16 models for a two‑constant, one‑relation language) and discusses when database semantics is appropriate. | Key concepts: First‑Order Logic (FOL), Standard semantics, Database semantics, Constant symbols, Relation symbols, Model (interpretation), Domain of discourse, Tuple, Knowledge base, Logic programming | Example questions: How does database semantics differ from the standard semantics of first‑order logic?; Why does a language with two constants and one binary relation have only 16 possible models under database semantics?

children.title: 8.4 Knowledge Engineering in First-Order Logic
children.abstract: This section explains how to build a knowledge base using first‑order logic, outlining the knowledge‑engineering process (identifying tasks, modeling the domain, defining axioms, etc.) and illustrating it with an electronic‑circuit example. It also contrasts special‑purpose knowledge bases with broader, general‑purpose ones. | Key concepts: Knowledge engineering, Knowledge base, First‑order logic, Axioms (including successor‑state axioms), Domain modeling, Special‑purpose knowledge base, General‑purpose knowledge base, Task identification, Representation of objects and relations | Example questions: What are the main steps involved in constructing a first‑order logic knowledge base?; How does a special‑purpose knowledge base differ from a general‑purpose knowledge base in terms of scope and query support?

children.title: 8.5 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes the key ideas introduced in the chapter on first‑order logic, emphasizing its advantages over propositional logic, the required syntactic extensions (terms, quantifiers), and the notion of a model that interprets symbols. It also touches on the historical development of relational logic and outlines the steps for building a first‑order knowledge base. | Key concepts: First‑order logic, Declarative knowledge representation, Ontological vs. epistemological commitments, Quantifiers (universal and existential), Model / possible world interpretation, Atomic sentence truth conditions, Vocabulary selection and axiom encoding, Aristotle’s logic, Relations (many‑place predicates), Knowledge base construction | Example questions: What are the main differences between propositional logic and first‑order logic in terms of expressive power and commitments?; How does a first‑order logic model assign meanings to constants, predicates, and functions, and how does this affect the truth of quantified sentences?

children.title: 9 Inference in First-Order Logic
children.abstract: This section introduces inference in first‑order logic, starting with basic quantifier inference rules that eliminate quantifiers and showing how first‑order inference can be reduced to propositional inference. It also outlines the motivation for more direct methods such as unification, forward and backward chaining, and resolution. | Key concepts: Universal quantifier inference rule, Existential quantifier inference rule, Quantifier elimination, Reduction to propositional inference, Unification, Horn clause, Forward chaining, Backward chaining, Resolution theorem proving | Example questions: How can we eliminate universal and existential quantifiers to turn a first‑order sentence into a quantifier‑free form?; Why is it possible to solve some first‑order inference problems by converting them to propositional logic, and what are the limitations of this approach?

children.title: 9.1 Propositional vs. First-Order Inference
children.abstract: Section 9.1 explains how inference with quantifiers works in first‑order logic, showing how universal and existential quantifiers can be eliminated using simple inference rules and how this reduction allows first‑order reasoning to be performed via propositional inference (though often inefficiently). It also sets the stage for more direct first‑order inference techniques such as unification. | Key concepts: Universal quantifier (∀), Existential quantifier (∃), Quantifier elimination, Propositional reduction, Soundness and completeness, Horn clause, First‑order inference, Resolution (preview), Unification (preview), Knowledge base conversion | Example questions: How can we remove universal quantifiers from a first‑order sentence to use propositional inference?; Why is converting a first‑order knowledge base to propositional form often impractical?

children.title: 9.2 Unification and Lifting
children.abstract: Section 9.2 introduces the mechanisms of unification and lifting that enable efficient first‑order inference without exhaustive propositionalization. It explains how substitutions (θ) can match rule premises to known facts, allowing conclusions to be drawn automatically, and shows how universal statements are handled through these techniques. | Key concepts: Unification, Substitution (θ), First‑order inference rule, Lifting, Universal quantification, Predicate logic, Resolution, Clause grounding | Example questions: How does unification allow a computer to infer Evil(John) from a rule about greedy kings?; What is the role of a substitution θ in the lifting process for first‑order logic inference?

children.title: 9.3 Forward Chaining
children.abstract: This section introduces forward chaining for first‑order definite clauses, extending the propositional forward‑chaining algorithm by applying Modus Ponens with variable substitution (unification). It explains the structure of first‑order definite clauses, how variables are implicitly universally quantified, and illustrates the method with a legal‑reasoning example. | Key concepts: Forward chaining, First‑order definite clause, Modus Ponens (forward direction), Unification, Universal quantification of variables, Antecedent (conjunction of positive literals), Consequent (single positive literal), Knowledge base (KB), Inference rule | Example questions: How does forward chaining work with first‑order definite clauses that contain variables?; What is the role of unification in applying Modus Ponens during forward chaining?

children.title: 9.4 Backward Chaining
children.abstract: This section introduces backward chaining as a goal‑driven inference method for definite clauses, presents the standard backward‑chaining algorithm (FOL‑BC‑ASK), and discusses its role in logic programming, its drawbacks relative to forward chaining, and its relationship to constraint‑satisfaction problems. | Key concepts: Backward chaining, Definite clauses, FOL‑BC‑ASK algorithm, AND/OR search, Logic programming, Generator (multiple solutions), Goal‑driven inference, Forward vs. backward inference, Constraint satisfaction problems | Example questions: How does the backward‑chaining algorithm FOL‑BC‑ASK work for proving a goal in a knowledge base of definite clauses?; What are the main advantages and disadvantages of backward chaining compared to forward chaining, and how does it relate to logic programming?

children.title: 9.5 Resolution
children.abstract: This section introduces resolution as a complete inference method for first‑order logic, building on the propositional resolution technique. It explains how to convert first‑order formulas to conjunctive normal form and outlines the role of resolution in logical systems alongside constraint logic programming. | Key concepts: Resolution (refutation), First‑order logic, Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF), Clause, Unification, Skolemization, Herbrand universe, Completeness of resolution, Constraint Logic Programming (CLP), Metarules for search control | Example questions: How does resolution work for first‑order logic and what steps are needed to apply it?; What is the process for converting a first‑order formula into conjunctive normal form before using resolution?

children.title: 9.6 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section reviews methods for performing logical inference in first‑order logic, covering rule‑based approaches, unification, generalized Modus Ponens, forward and backward chaining, Datalog and Prolog characteristics, and resolution with strategies to prune the search space. | Key concepts: Universal and Existential Instantiation, Unification, Generalized Modus Ponens (Lifted Modus Ponens), Forward Chaining, Backward Chaining, Datalog (function‑free definite clauses), Prolog (closed‑world assumption, negation as failure), Generalized Resolution, Search‑space reduction strategies | Example questions: How does unification improve the efficiency of first‑order logic inference compared to simple instantiation?; What are the main differences between forward chaining and backward chaining, and where are they each applied (e.g., Datalog vs. Prolog)?

children.title: 10 Classical Planning
children.abstract: This section introduces classical planning, a framework for generating action sequences that achieve goals in fully observable, deterministic, static environments. It presents a constrained yet expressive representation for planning problems, explains how forward and backward search can exploit this representation using automatically derived heuristics, and outlines the role of planning graphs in making search more efficient. | Key concepts: Classical planning, Planning problem representation, Forward search, Backward (regression) search, Domain‑independent heuristics, Planning graph, Fully observable deterministic environment, State space, Action schema | Example questions: How does classical planning differ from the search‑based problem‑solving agent described earlier?; What are the main advantages of using a planning graph when searching for a plan?

children.title: 10.1 Definition of Classical Planning
children.abstract: Section 10.1 introduces the formal definition of classical planning, describing the assumptions (fully observable, deterministic, static, single‑agent) and the language used to model planning problems. It contrasts classical planning with earlier problem‑solving approaches, highlighting the need for a structured representation that enables domain‑independent heuristics and efficient plan generation. | Key concepts: Classical planning, Fully observable deterministic environment, Planning problem representation, State space, Action schema, Preconditions and effects, Goal state, Domain‑independent heuristics, Ground (variable‑free) propositional inference | Example questions: What are the core assumptions that define a classical planning problem?; How does the representation of actions in classical planning differ from the atomic state representations used in earlier problem‑solving agents?

children.title: 10.2 Algorithms for Planning as State-Space Search
children.abstract: This section explains how classical planning problems can be treated as state‑space search problems and compares two fundamental approaches: forward (progression) search from the initial state and backward (regression) search from the goal. It discusses why early planners considered forward search inefficient, highlighting issues such as the exploration of irrelevant actions. | Key concepts: Planning problem, State‑space search, Forward (progression) search, Backward (regression) search, Action schema, Initial state, Goal state, Heuristic search, Irrelevant actions, Search efficiency | Example questions: What are the main differences between forward (progression) and backward (regression) search in classical planning?; Why was forward state‑space search considered inefficient in early planning research?

children.title: 10.3 Planning Graphs
children.abstract: This section introduces planning graphs as a compact, polynomial‑size approximation of the exponential search tree used in classical planning. It explains how planning graphs support more accurate heuristics (e.g., the ignore‑delete‑lists heuristic used by the FF planner) and can also serve as the basis for the GRAPHPLAN algorithm. | Key concepts: Planning Graph, Heuristic Estimation, Ignore‑Delete‑Lists Heuristic, FF (Fast‑Forward) Planner, Hill‑Climbing Search with Restarts, Iterative Deepening Search, GRAPHPLAN Algorithm, Polynomial‑size Approximation, Goal Reachability Estimation | Example questions: How does a planning graph improve heuristic estimates compared to simpler heuristics?; What role does the planning graph play in the FF planner’s search strategy?

children.title: 10.4 Other Classical Planning Approaches
children.abstract: This section surveys alternative classical planning methods beyond the three dominant approaches (SAT encoding, forward state‑space search with heuristics, and planning‑graph search). It reviews historic top‑performing planners from the International Planning Competition and introduces three influential paradigms: planning as first‑order logical deduction, planning as constraint satisfaction, and plan refinement. | Key concepts: International Planning Competition (IPC), Optimal vs. Satisficing tracks, SATPLAN (Boolean satisfiability encoding), LAMA (fast downward search with FF heuristic), FF (forward search planner), Planning graph (e.g., IPP, HSP), First‑order logical deduction planning, Constraint‑satisfaction planning, Plan refinement, Hand‑coded vs. Automated heuristics | Example questions: What are some of the alternative classical planning approaches that were explored before the current dominant methods?; How did the International Planning Competition influence the development of planners like SATPLAN, LAMA, and FF?

children.title: 10.5 Analysis of Planning Approaches
children.abstract: This section examines how different planning techniques manage the combinatorial complexity of AI planning, highlighting the role of problem decomposition, mutex detection, and heuristic search. It compares approaches such as Graphplan, SATPlan, and forward‑search planners, and introduces the notion of serializable subgoals as a way to exploit partial independence among goals. | Key concepts: Combinatorial explosion, Problem decomposability, Mutex (mutual exclusion) relations, Graphplan, SATPlan, Forward search heuristics, Serializable subgoals, PSPACE‑hardness of planning | Example questions: How do Graphplan and SATPlan detect and use mutex relations to improve planning efficiency?; What does it mean for a planning problem to have serializable subgoals, and why is this useful?

children.title: 10.6 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes the core ideas of deterministic planning covered in the chapter, outlining the PDDL formalism, major algorithmic strategies (state‑space search, planning graphs, SAT/CSP encodings, situation‑calculus deduction, and partial‑order planning), and the role of heuristics and mutex relations. It also gives brief bibliographic and historical context for the field. | Key concepts: Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL), State‑space search (forward progression and backward regression), Heuristics derived from subgoal independence and relaxations, Planning graph and mutex (mutual exclusion) relations, GRAPHPLAN algorithm, First‑order deduction / situation calculus, Encoding planning as Boolean SAT, Encoding planning as Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP), Partial‑order planning | Example questions: What is PDDL and how does it specify the initial state, goal state, and actions in a planning problem?; How does a planning graph generate useful heuristics and what are mutex relations?

children.title: 11 Planning and Acting in the Real World
children.abstract: This section explains how planning systems are extended for real‑world use by incorporating temporal information, resource constraints, hierarchical decomposition, and interactive agent architectures. It introduces richer planning languages that handle action durations and schedules, discusses hierarchical planning to capture expert knowledge, and outlines architectures that interleave planning with execution in uncertain, multi‑agent environments. | Key concepts: Temporal planning, Scheduling, Resource constraints, Hierarchical planning, Abstract task decomposition, Deliberation‑execution interleaving, Uncertain environments, Multi‑agent planning, Agent architectures | Example questions: How do planners represent action durations and resource limits when creating schedules for real‑world problems?; What is hierarchical planning and why does it make plan construction more efficient in complex domains?

children.title: 11.1 Time, Schedules, and Resources
children.abstract: Section 11.1 extends the classical planning model by introducing temporal information and resource constraints, enabling planners to generate schedules that specify when actions occur and how long they last. It explains how to represent actions with durations, deadlines, and limited resources, and outlines basic methods for solving such time‑ and resource‑aware planning problems. | Key concepts: Temporal planning, Action duration, Scheduling, Resource constraints, Makespan, Deadlines, Temporal constraints (e.g., before, after, overlap), Resource allocation, Time windows, Concurrent actions | Example questions: How can a planner represent the length of an action and ensure that resources aren’t double‑booked?; What is the difference between classical planning and temporal planning with scheduling constraints?

children.title: 11.2 Hierarchical Planning
children.abstract: Section 11.2 explains why planning must be performed at multiple levels of abstraction, introducing hierarchical planning as a way to manage the combinatorial explosion of low‑level actions. It illustrates how high‑level goals (e.g., a vacation itinerary) can be recursively decomposed into sub‑tasks until primitive actions suitable for execution are reached, and notes that planning can interleave with execution. | Key concepts: Hierarchical planning, Abstraction levels, Atomic actions, Task decomposition, Recursive sub‑task planning, Interleaved planning and execution, Planning horizon, Motor control sequences | Example questions: Why do AI systems need hierarchical planning instead of planning with only primitive actions?; How does hierarchical planning allow a plan to be refined during execution?

children.title: 11.3 Planning and Acting in Nondeterministic Domains
children.abstract: Section 11.3 expands classical planning to environments that are partially observable, nondeterministic, or completely unknown. It introduces techniques such as sensorless (conformant) planning, contingency planning, and the angelic search framework that use optimistic and pessimistic abstractions to generate abstract, cost‑bounded plans and hierarchical look‑ahead strategies. | Key concepts: Nondeterministic planning, Partially observable domains, Conformant (sensorless) planning, Contingency planning, Angelic search, Optimistic and pessimistic abstractions, Reachable‑set cost bounds, Hierarchical lookahead (LRTA*), Abstract plan refinement | Example questions: How can we create a plan when the environment is nondeterministic and we have no sensors?; What is the angelic approach and how does it help compute optimal abstract plans in uncertain domains?

children.title: 11.4 Multiagent Planning
children.abstract: This section discusses how agents can monitor and replan their actions in multi‑agent environments, addressing challenges such as dead‑ends, hidden preconditions, and nondeterministic outcomes. It highlights the importance of model learning from prediction failures to improve repair planning and ensure eventual goal achievement. | Key concepts: Plan monitoring, Replanning, Dead‑end states, Nondeterministic actions, Hidden preconditions, Repair plan selection, Model learning, Partial‑order planning, Planning‑graph planners, State‑space planners | Example questions: How can an agent guarantee eventual goal achievement when its actions are nondeterministic or when hidden preconditions cause failures?; What role does learning a better world model play in improving an agent's ability to repair failed plans?

children.title: 11.5 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: Section 11.5 reviews the challenges of planning and acting in real‑world, multi‑agent environments. It highlights how resources are modeled as numeric pools, discusses emergent collective behaviors such as Reynolds' boids, and notes the difficulty of coordinated planning when agents must both cooperate with teammates and compete against opponents without centralized control. | Key concepts: Resource pools, Emergent behavior, Reynolds' boids model, Cohesion, Separation, Alignment, Loose coupling, Multi‑agent cooperation and competition, Centralized vs. decentralized control, Planning under resource constraints | Example questions: How does the boids model achieve flocking behavior using cohesion, separation, and alignment?; Why are resource pools preferred over tracking individual items when planning actions in the real world?

children.title: 12 Knowledge Representation
children.abstract: This section introduces knowledge representation using first‑order logic, focusing on how to structure an agent's knowledge base with an ontological hierarchy. It outlines the need for general, flexible representations of abstract concepts such as events, time, objects, and beliefs, and sets the stage for reasoning techniques that will be covered later. | Key concepts: First‑order logic, Ontology, Ontological engineering, Categories (hierarchy), Physical objects, Events, Time, Beliefs, Knowledge base | Example questions: What is ontological engineering and why is it important for complex domains?; How does the chapter propose organizing knowledge about events, time, and objects in a knowledge base?

children.title: 12.1 Ontological Engineering
children.abstract: Section 12.1 introduces ontological engineering, explaining how to build a general, hierarchical ontology that organizes world knowledge into categories such as objects, events, time, and beliefs. It emphasizes the need for flexible, reusable representations for complex domains like Internet shopping or autonomous driving, and shows how to create placeholders for domain‑specific knowledge within a universal framework. | Key concepts: Ontology, Hierarchical categorization, General concepts (Events, Time, Physical Objects, Beliefs), Ontological engineering, Domain‑independent representation, Placeholders for domain‑specific knowledge, Knowledge base design, First‑order logic representation | Example questions: What is ontological engineering and why is it important for building knowledge bases in complex domains?; How does a hierarchical ontology help organize concepts like events, time, and objects for applications such as Internet shopping?

children.title: 12.2 Categories and Objects
children.abstract: This section explains how objects are organized into categories for knowledge representation, highlighting the role of categories in reasoning, prediction, and inheritance. It contrasts two ways to represent categories in first‑order logic—using predicates versus reified category objects—and introduces the concepts of membership, subcategory (subclass), and inheritance within a taxonomy. | Key concepts: Category, Reification, Membership (Member / ∈), Subcategory / Subclass / Subset, Inheritance, Taxonomy, Predicate representation, Object representation | Example questions: How can a category be represented in first‑order logic, and what is the difference between using a predicate and reifying the category as an object?; What does inheritance mean in the context of categories, and how does it allow us to infer properties of specific objects?

children.title: 12.3 Events
children.abstract: This section introduces the Event Calculus as an alternative to Situation Calculus for representing actions that are continuous, overlapping, or simultaneous.
