It defines how fluents, events, time intervals, and a set of predicates (T, Happens, Initiates, Extent) are used to model when facts hold and how events cause changes over time. | Key concepts: Event Calculus, Fluent, Event, T(f, t) predicate, Happens(e, i) predicate, Initiates(e, f, t) predicate, Extent(e) = i, Time interval (start, end), Situation Calculus (contrast), Event category (e.g., Flyings) | Example questions: How does Event Calculus allow us to represent actions that occur over a period of time, unlike Situation Calculus?; What predicates are used in Event Calculus to state that a fluent holds at a specific time and that an event causes a fluent to become true?

children.title: 12.4 Mental Events and Mental Objects
children.abstract: This section introduces a formal model for representing mental objects (such as beliefs) and mental events (such as reasoning processes) within an agent’s knowledge base, emphasizing meta‑knowledge—knowledge about one’s own and others’ knowledge and reasoning. It explains why special constructs (e.g., the T predicate and the Equals function) are needed to capture temporal identity and the dynamics of mental states. | Key concepts: Mental objects, Mental events, Meta‑knowledge, Belief representation, Deduction as a mental event, Temporal identity (Equals vs. =), T predicate (time‑indexed truth), Epistemic reasoning about others, Knowledge about one’s own reasoning | Example questions: How does the formalism distinguish between logical identity and time‑dependent identity of objects like President(USA)?; Why do we need a separate construct for representing an agent’s knowledge about its own beliefs and reasoning processes?

children.title: 12.5 Reasoning Systems for Categories
children.abstract: This section introduces modal logic as a formalism for representing knowledge and belief in reasoning systems, presenting basic axioms such as knowledge closure under implication, truthfulness of knowledge, and positive introspection. It also discusses the limitation of logical omniscience inherent in these modal approaches, especially when modeling realistic agents. | Key concepts: Modal operator for knowledge (K), Knowledge closure axiom (KaP ∧ Ka(P ⇒ Q) ⇒ KaQ), Truth axiom (KaP ⇒ P), Positive introspection (KaP ⇒ Ka(KaP)), Logical omniscience, Belief modality (B), Quantified knowledge (∃x KBondSpy(x) vs. KBond∃x Spy(x)), Accessible worlds semantics, Justified true belief | Example questions: How does modal logic formalize the difference between "knowing that there exists a spy" and "knowing who the spy is"?; Why is logical omniscience considered a problem for knowledge and belief representations in AI reasoning systems?

children.title: 12.6 Reasoning with Default Information
children.abstract: Section 12.6 introduces non‑monotonic reasoning techniques for handling default information, explaining how defaults can be overridden by more specific facts. It covers the formal semantics of defaults through circumscription and default logic, and relates these ideas to inheritance in semantic networks and the closed‑world assumption. | Key concepts: Default information, Inheritance and overriding, Circumscription, Default logic, Monotonicity vs. non‑monotonic reasoning, Closed‑world assumption, Semantic networks, Description logics, Non‑monotonic reasoning | Example questions: How do circumscription and default logic formalize the idea that defaults can be overridden by more specific information?; Why does reasoning with defaults violate the monotonicity property of classical logic?

children.title: 12.7 The Internet Shopping World
children.abstract: This section explains how Assumption‑based Truth Maintenance Systems (ATMS) manage multiple hypothetical worlds by labeling sentences with sets of assumptions, contrasting them with Justification‑based TMS (JTMS). It also describes how ATMS generates explanations—sets of sentences (including assumptions) that entail a target sentence—and the preference for minimal explanations. | Key concepts: Assumption‑based Truth Maintenance System (ATMS), Justification‑based Truth Maintenance System (JTMS), Assumption set / label, Hypothetical world switching, Explanation (entailment), Assumption (as a provisional truth), Minimal explanation, Contradictory assumptions handling | Example questions: How does an ATMS differ from a JTMS in representing multiple possible states?; What is a minimal explanation in a truth maintenance system and how is it derived?

children.title: 12.8 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: Section 12.8 summarizes how a shopping agent extracts and compares offers for products with multiple attributes, introducing the notion of dominance among offers and explaining that the agent returns all undominated offers that satisfy the buyer's description. It also notes the need for user‑specific preference weighting for attributes that are not universally comparable. | Key concepts: Offer extraction, Attribute comparison, Dominance (dominated vs. undominated offers), Multi‑attribute preferences, Declarative construction of agents, Domain‑specific knowledge, User‑specified weighting, Price‑performance trade‑off | Example questions: How does the shopping agent decide which laptop offers to present to the user?; What does it mean for one offer to dominate another in the context of multi‑attribute product comparison?

chapters.title: IV: Uncertain knowledge and reasoning
chapters.abstract: This section explains why purely logical belief‑state representations struggle with uncertainty and introduces the need for quantitative approaches (degrees of belief) to act under partial observability and nondeterminism. It discusses the limitations of exhaustive contingency planning and motivates probabilistic reasoning for comparing imperfect plans. | Key concepts: Uncertainty, Partial observability, Nondeterminism, Belief state, Contingency plan, Degrees of belief, Probabilistic reasoning, Plan evaluation under uncertainty, Explosive combinatorial growth | Example questions: Why can’t a logical agent that tracks all possible world states reliably choose a plan when the environment is uncertain?; How do degrees of belief help an agent compare plans that are not guaranteed to succeed?

children.title: 13 Quantifying Uncertainty
children.abstract: This section introduces how intelligent agents can manage uncertainty by moving from binary logical reasoning to quantitative degrees of belief. It discusses the limitations of pure belief‑state and contingency‑plan approaches and motivates the need for probabilistic representations and decision‑theoretic evaluation of actions. | Key concepts: Uncertainty, Partial observability, Nondeterminism, Belief state, Contingency plan, Degrees of belief, Logical agent, Plan evaluation under uncertainty, Probabilistic reasoning | Example questions: Why can’t a logical agent that uses belief states always guarantee a correct plan in uncertain environments?; What is meant by ‘degrees of belief’ and how does it help an agent act when its sensors give incomplete information?

children.title: 13.1 Acting under Uncertainty
children.abstract: This section explains why purely logical agents that rely on exhaustive belief‑state representations and contingency plans struggle with uncertainty caused by partial observability and nondeterminism. It motivates the need for quantitative approaches—such as degrees of belief—to compare and choose among plans that are not guaranteed to succeed. | Key concepts: Belief state, Partial observability, Nondeterminism, Contingency plan, Logical agent, Uncertainty, Degrees of belief, Probabilistic reasoning, Plan evaluation under uncertainty, Automated taxi example | Example questions: Why can’t a logical agent that tracks all possible world states always find a guaranteed plan?; How do degrees of belief help an agent choose between plans when outcomes are uncertain?

children.title: 13.2 Basic Probability Notation
children.abstract: Section 13.2 introduces the basic notation and concepts of probability as they relate to decision theory, explaining how utilities represent an agent's preferences and how these utilities are combined with probabilities to evaluate actions. It defines the principle of maximum expected utility, which states that a rational agent selects the action with the highest expected (probability‑weighted) utility. | Key concepts: Utility, Utility function, Preferences, Probability theory, Decision theory, Maximum Expected Utility (MEU), Expected utility, Rational agent | Example questions: What does the principle of maximum expected utility (MEU) mean in decision theory?; How does decision theory combine probability theory and utility theory to guide an agent's choices?

children.title: 13.3 Inference Using Full Joint Distributions
children.abstract: This section explains how full joint probability distributions provide a coherent basis for inference, illustrating why beliefs must obey the probability axioms through de Finetti’s betting (Dutch‑book) argument and related philosophical justifications (Cox, Carnap, Jaynes). It shows that inconsistent belief assignments lead to guaranteed losses, reinforcing the necessity of probabilistic coherence. | Key concepts: Full joint distribution, De Finetti’s theorem, Dutch‑book argument, Coherence (probabilistic consistency), Probability axioms, Cox’s theorem, Carnap’s logical probability, Jaynes’ Bayesian reasoning, Belief degrees as numbers, Betting interpretation of uncertainty | Example questions: Why does an agent with incoherent probability assignments always lose in a betting scenario?; How does de Finetti’s theorem justify using full joint probability distributions for inference?

children.title: 13.4 Independence
children.abstract: This section introduces the concept of probabilistic independence and shows how it can be used to factor a large joint probability distribution into smaller, more manageable tables. By assuming that certain variables (e.g., weather and dental symptoms) do not influence each other, the full distribution can be expressed as the product of marginal distributions, dramatically reducing the amount of data needed. | Key concepts: Independence (probabilistic), Joint probability distribution, Product rule, Conditional probability, Factorization of distributions, Marginal distribution, Dimensionality reduction (O(2ⁿ) vs. smaller tables), Assumption of independence, Bayesian network intuition | Example questions: How does assuming independence between two variables simplify the representation of a joint probability table?; What equation lets us express P(Toothache, Catch, Cavity, Weather) as the product of smaller distributions?

children.title: 13.5 Bayes’ Rule and Its Use
children.abstract: This section introduces Bayes’ rule, deriving it from the product rule and explaining its central role in probabilistic inference. It also discusses how independence can be used to factor large joint distributions into smaller, more manageable pieces, illustrating the concepts with examples from weather‑dental problems and independent coin flips. | Key concepts: Product rule, Bayes’ rule (Bayes’ theorem), Conditional probability, Joint distribution, Independence (absolute independence), Factorization of joint distributions, Probabilistic inference, Variable subsets | Example questions: How is Bayes’ rule derived from the product rule and what does it allow us to compute?; Why does independence enable us to factor a large joint probability distribution into smaller ones?

children.title: 13.6 The Wumpus World Revisited
children.abstract: This section explains how conditional independence dramatically reduces the size of probabilistic representations, using the dentistry example to illustrate the naive Bayes model where a single cause influences multiple independent effects. It highlights the O(n) versus O(2ⁿ) scaling advantage and notes that naive Bayes often works well even when its independence assumptions are only approximate. | Key concepts: Conditional independence, Naive Bayes model, Joint probability factorization, Scaling of probability tables (O(n) vs O(2ⁿ)), Independent numbers in CPTs, Cause‑effect relationships, Bayesian classifier (idiot Bayes), Probabilistic representation size | Example questions: How does assuming conditional independence reduce the number of parameters needed in a Bayesian network?; Why is the naive Bayes model called 'naive' and when can it still perform well despite its assumptions?

children.title: 13.7 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: Section 13.7 reviews the key ideas introduced in the chapter on uncertain knowledge and reasoning, emphasizing probability theory as the foundation for representing uncertainty, the role of decision theory in choosing actions, and the challenges of scaling full joint distributions. It also highlights how independence assumptions—absolute and conditional—enable factorization of the joint distribution, with Bayes' rule and the naive Bayes model as central tools. | Key concepts: Probability theory, Uncertainty (laziness and ignorance), Prior and conditional probabilities, Decision theory and expected utility, Full joint probability distribution, Absolute independence, Conditional independence, Bayes' rule, Naive Bayes model | Example questions: How does Bayes' rule help compute unknown probabilities from known conditional probabilities?; Why is the full joint probability distribution usually impractical to use directly, and how do independence assumptions alleviate this problem?

children.title: 14 Probabilistic Reasoning
children.abstract: This section introduces Bayesian networks as a compact representation for joint probability distributions, explaining their syntax, semantics, and how they exploit (conditional) independence to model uncertain knowledge. It also outlines exact and approximate inference methods and briefly touches on extensions to first‑order representations and alternative uncertainty frameworks. | Key concepts: Bayesian network, Joint probability distribution, Conditional independence, Exact probabilistic inference, Approximate inference algorithms, First‑order probabilistic models, Independence assumptions, Network semantics (nodes and directed edges), Inference tractability | Example questions: How do Bayesian networks use conditional independence to reduce the size of a joint probability table?; What are the main differences between exact and approximate inference methods in Bayesian networks?

children.title: 14.1 Representing Knowledge in an Uncertain Domain
children.abstract: This section introduces Bayesian networks as a compact data structure for representing probabilistic knowledge in domains with uncertainty. It explains how independence and conditional independence allow the full joint distribution to be encoded efficiently, and outlines the basics of inference and its computational challenges. | Key concepts: Bayesian network, Full joint probability distribution, Independence, Conditional independence, Network syntax and semantics, Probabilistic inference, Exact vs. approximate inference, First‑order probabilistic representations, Alternative uncertain‑reasoning approaches | Example questions: How do Bayesian networks use conditional independence to reduce the number of probabilities needed to specify a joint distribution?; Why is exact probabilistic inference often intractable, and what kinds of approximate methods can be used instead?

children.title: 14.2 The Semantics of Bayesian Networks
children.abstract: This section explains the meaning (semantics) of Bayesian networks, showing that they can be understood either as a compact representation of a full joint probability distribution or as an encoding of a set of conditional independence assertions. It highlights how these two views are equivalent and why each is useful for building networks and designing inference algorithms. | Key concepts: Bayesian network, Directed acyclic graph (DAG), Joint probability distribution, Conditional independence, Parameters θ (or CPT entries), Parents(Xi), Semantics of a network, Inference procedures, Conditional probability table (CPT), Equivalence of representations | Example questions: How does a Bayesian network represent the full joint distribution of its variables?; What is the relationship between the graph structure of a Bayesian network and conditional independence statements?

children.title: 14.3 Efficient Representation of Conditional Distributions
children.abstract: This section explains how to avoid the exponential blow‑up of full conditional probability tables by using compact, canonical representations such as deterministic and other standard distributions. It shows how conditional independence and the Markov blanket let us specify a node’s behavior with far fewer parameters than the worst‑case O(2^k) table. | Key concepts: Conditional Probability Table (CPT), Canonical distribution, Deterministic node, Conditional independence, Markov blanket, Parent nodes, Exponential parameter growth (O(2^k)), Logical relationships (e.g., OR, AND), Numerical relationships (e.g., sum, min, max) | Example questions: How can we represent a node’s conditional distribution without enumerating all 2^k entries in its CPT?; What is a deterministic node and how does it simplify the specification of conditional probabilities in a Bayesian network?

children.title: 14.4 Exact Inference in Bayesian Networks
children.abstract: This section introduces exact inference in Bayesian networks, explaining how to compute posterior probability distributions for query variables given observed evidence. It presents the formal notation (X, E, e) and outlines the fundamental algorithms—enumeration and variable elimination—that perform these calculations efficiently. | Key concepts: Bayesian network, Exact inference, Posterior probability, Query variable (X), Evidence variables (E) and observed event (e), Enumeration algorithm, Variable elimination, Factor (intermediate table), Conditional probability table (CPT), Computational complexity of inference | Example questions: How can I compute P(X | e) for a single query variable in a Bayesian network?; What is the variable‑elimination algorithm and how does it differ from simple enumeration?

children.title: 14.5 Approximate Inference in Bayesian Networks
children.abstract: This section explains why exact inference in large, multiply‑connected Bayesian networks is often infeasible and introduces approximate inference techniques based on Monte Carlo sampling. It covers two main families—direct (forward) sampling and Markov‑chain sampling—and briefly mentions other approaches such as variational methods and loopy belief propagation. | Key concepts: Monte Carlo sampling, Approximate inference, Direct (forward) sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), Posterior probability estimation, Intractability of exact inference, Variable elimination, Clustered (polytree) networks, Variational methods, Loopy belief propagation | Example questions: How can we estimate posterior probabilities in a Bayesian network when exact inference is computationally prohibitive?; What are the differences between direct sampling and Markov chain sampling for approximate inference?

children.title: 14.6 Relational and First-Order Probability Models
children.abstract: This section introduces relational and first‑order probability models, showing how Bayesian networks can be extended with the expressive power of first‑order logic to represent uncertain knowledge about multiple objects and their relationships. It explains the motivation, basic structure (template or lifted Bayes nets), and the advantages of using such models for domains like recommendation systems where the number of entities varies. | Key concepts: Relational Bayesian Network (Template Bayes Net), First‑Order Probability Model, Grounding (Instantiation of Template Variables), Lifted Inference, Parameterized Random Variable (PRV), Object and Relation Types, Domain Lifted Representation, Evidence Propagation in Relational Models, Scalability via Sharing of Parameters | Example questions: How can Bayesian networks be adapted to handle domains with an unknown number of objects, such as many customers recommending many books?; What is the difference between grounding a relational Bayes net and performing lifted inference, and why does the latter improve efficiency?

children.title: 14.7 Other Approaches to Uncertain Reasoning
children.abstract: This section surveys alternative methods for handling uncertainty in AI, focusing on probabilistic approaches such as open‑universe first‑order models and Markov chain Monte Carlo inference. It highlights the historical preference for probability in other sciences and notes the growing impact of first‑order probabilistic reasoning on AI applications. | Key concepts: Probabilistic Reasoning, Open‑universe Models, First‑order Probabilistic Logic, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), Partial World Sampling, Acyclicity and Well‑Foundedness, Posterior Distribution, Uncertain Knowledge Representation | Example questions: How do open‑universe probabilistic models handle inference when the number of objects is unbounded?; Why is MCMC sampling used for first‑order probabilistic reasoning, and what challenges does it face?

children.title: 14.8 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section discusses how fuzzy logic can be interpreted through probabilistic frameworks, including hidden‑variable models, random sets, and hybrid Bayesian networks, and it critiques the practical success of fuzzy systems as stemming from their simplicity rather than their fuzzy operators. | Key concepts: Fuzzy predicates, Probabilistic interpretation of fuzzy logic, Hidden continuous variables, Hybrid Bayesian network, Random sets, Probit distribution, Truth‑functional vs. probabilistic reasoning, Critiques of fuzzy system design | Example questions: How can a statement like 'Nate is tall' be modeled using probability theory instead of fuzzy logic?; What is the role of random sets in giving a probabilistic meaning to fuzzy predicates?

children.title: 15 Probabilistic Reasoning over Time
children.abstract: This section introduces probabilistic reasoning over time, showing how agents can maintain and update belief states using probability theory in partially observable environments. It covers temporal modeling with transition and sensor models, defines core inference tasks, and presents three main frameworks—hidden Markov models, Kalman filters, and dynamic Bayesian networks. | Key concepts: Belief state, Transition model, Sensor model, Hidden Markov model (HMM), Kalman filter, Dynamic Bayesian network (DBN), Temporal inference, Partial observability, Probability distribution over states | Example questions: How do hidden Markov models differ from Kalman filters in representing uncertainty over time?; What is the role of a sensor model when updating an agent's belief state in a partially observable environment?

children.title: 15.1 Time and Uncertainty
children.abstract: Section 15.1 introduces probabilistic reasoning over time, showing how agents can maintain and update belief states using probability theory instead of just possible-world sets. It explains how transition and sensor models are expressed as probability distributions over variables indexed by time, laying the groundwork for temporal inference methods such as hidden Markov models, Kalman filters, and dynamic Bayesian networks. | Key concepts: Belief state, Transition model, Sensor model, Probability distribution, Temporal variable indexing, Hidden Markov model (HMM), Kalman filter, Dynamic Bayesian network (DBN), Partial observability | Example questions: How does a probabilistic transition model differ from the deterministic one used in earlier chapters?; What role do belief states play in hidden Markov models and Kalman filters?

children.title: 15.2 Inference in Temporal Models
children.abstract: Section 15.2 discusses how to perform inference in temporal probabilistic models, focusing on the trade‑offs between increasing model order versus expanding the set of state variables to preserve the Markov property. It illustrates these ideas with examples such as weather prediction and robot tracking, emphasizing the need for a self‑sufficient set of variables and the role of additional sensors in improving predictive accuracy. | Key concepts: Temporal probabilistic models, Markov property, State variables, Model order, Self‑sufficient variable set, Sensor augmentation, Inference over time, Dynamic Bayesian networks | Example questions: How can we restore the Markov property in a robot tracking model when battery level affects motion?; What is the difference between increasing the order of a temporal model and adding new state variables?

children.title: 15.3 Hidden Markov Models
children.abstract: This section introduces Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) and explains how to find the most likely sequence of hidden states using the Viterbi algorithm, a dynamic‑programming variant of the forward algorithm that replaces summations with maximizations. It also discusses the algorithm’s linear time and space complexity and the need to store back‑pointers to reconstruct the optimal state path. | Key concepts: Hidden Markov Model (HMM), Viterbi algorithm, Forward message (filtering), Max‑product (maximization) recursion, Most likely state sequence (MAP path), Dynamic programming, Back‑pointers (traceback), Time complexity O(t), Space complexity O(t), Transition and sensor models | Example questions: How does the Viterbi algorithm differ from the standard forward filtering algorithm in an HMM?; What is the computational complexity of finding the most probable sequence of hidden states in a Hidden Markov Model?

children.title: 15.4 Kalman Filters
children.abstract: This section introduces Kalman filtering as a method for estimating continuous‑valued state variables (such as position and velocity) from noisy, time‑sequential observations. It explains the linear‑Gaussian assumptions that make the filter tractable, shows how the state transition and observation models are expressed as Gaussian distributions, and outlines the recursive prediction‑update cycle that yields optimal estimates under these assumptions. | Key concepts: Kalman filter, Linear Gaussian model, State transition model, Observation (sensor) model, Recursive prediction‑update cycle, Gaussian noise, Hidden Markov model (continuous analogue), Covariance matrix, Optimal linear estimator | Example questions: How does a Kalman filter combine a motion model and noisy sensor readings to estimate a object's position over time?; Why does the Kalman filter assume linear Gaussian dynamics, and what are the key steps in its prediction and update phases?

children.title: 15.5 Dynamic Bayesian Networks
children.abstract: This section introduces Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) as temporal extensions of Bayesian networks, explaining how they model sequences of variables over time using repeated slices and first‑order Markov assumptions. It shows how DBNs generalize hidden Markov models and Kalman filters, and discusses the incorporation of discrete maneuver variables for switching models. | Key concepts: Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN), First‑order Markov process, Slice (time slice), State variable (Xt), Evidence variable (Et), Hidden Markov Model (HMM) equivalence, Kalman filter as a DBN, Switching Kalman filter, Maneuver state variable, Temporal replication of structure | Example questions: How does a Dynamic Bayesian Network differ from a standard Bayesian network, and what assumptions does it make about time?; In what way can a hidden Markov model be represented as a DBN, and how can multiple state variables be combined into a single HMM state?

children.title: 15.6 Keeping Track of Many Objects
children.abstract: This section explains how particle filtering works for state estimation, showing how samples are propagated, weighted, and resampled to approximate the forward message, and then extends the discussion to the challenges of tracking multiple objects simultaneously. | Key concepts: Particle filtering, Forward message (belief) propagation, Transition probability, Sensor (observation) model, Importance weighting, Resampling step, Bounded error guarantees, Multi‑object tracking, Data association | Example questions: How does particle filtering maintain a correct approximation of the posterior after each update cycle?; What additional difficulties arise when using particle filters to track more than one object at the same time?

children.title: 15.7 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes the key ideas from the chapter on probabilistic temporal processes, covering how random variables model changing world states, the use of Markov and stationarity assumptions, the roles of transition and sensor models, core inference tasks (filtering, prediction, smoothing, MAP), major model families (HMMs, Kalman filters, dynamic Bayesian networks), the difficulty of exact inference for large state spaces, and the importance of particle filtering and data‑association in multi‑object tracking. | Key concepts: Markov property, Stationary process, Transition model, Sensor model, Filtering, Prediction, Smoothing, Most likely explanation (MAP), Hidden Markov Model (HMM), Kalman filter | Example questions: What are the main inference tasks in temporal probabilistic models and how are they computed efficiently?; Why is exact inference often intractable for large temporal models, and what approximate method is commonly used?

children.title: 16 Making Simple Decisions
children.abstract: This section introduces decision theory as the framework for agents to choose actions that maximize expected utility, combining probabilistic beliefs with utility-based desires. It explains how utility functions capture preferences, how expected utility is computed, and how decision networks (influence diagrams) extend Bayesian networks to model actions and outcomes under uncertainty. | Key concepts: Expected Utility, Utility Function, Decision Theory, Rational Agent, Probabilistic Belief, Decision Network (Influence Diagram), Bayesian Network, Nondeterministic Environment, Partially Observable State, Goal‑Based vs. Utility‑Based Agent | Example questions: How does an agent decide which action to take when outcomes are uncertain?; What is the role of a decision network in combining probabilities and utilities?

children.title: 16.1 Combining Beliefs and Desires under Uncertainty
children.abstract: Section 16.1 introduces the core principle of decision theory—maximizing expected utility—as a way to integrate an agent's probabilistic beliefs with its desirability preferences (utilities). It explains how this framework extends simple goal‑based reasoning to handle uncertainty, nondeterministic outcomes, and partially observable environments. | Key concepts: Expected Utility, Utility Function, Decision Theory, Probability Theory, Rational Agent, Goal‑Based Agent, Nondeterministic Environment, Partially Observable Environment, Decision Network (Influence Diagram) | Example questions: How does a decision‑theoretic agent choose actions when outcomes are uncertain?; What is the role of expected utility in combining an agent's beliefs and desires?

children.title: 16.2 The Basis of Utility Theory
children.abstract: This section introduces the foundations of utility theory for decision‑making under uncertainty, defining utility functions, expected utility, and the principle of maximum expected utility (MEU). It also discusses how applying MEU connects to broader AI challenges such as perception, learning, causal modeling, and planning. | Key concepts: Utility Function (U(s)), Expected Utility (EU(a|e)), Maximum Expected Utility (MEU) Principle, Result(a) – outcome of an action, Probability Distribution P(RESULT(a)=s'|a,e), Causal Model of the World, Bayesian Network Inference, Performance Measure, Rational Agent | Example questions: How does the maximum expected utility principle determine which action an agent should take?; What components are needed to compute the expected utility of an action in a uncertain environment?

children.title: 16.3 Utility Functions
children.abstract: This section introduces utility functions as mappings from lotteries to real numbers and discusses how rational agents' preferences can be captured by such functions. It explains the need for utility assessment (preference elicitation) and how to establish a utility scale, often by normalizing utilities between a worst (0) and best (1) outcome. | Key concepts: Utility function, Lottery, Preference elicitation, Utility scale, Normalized utilities, Best possible prize (u⊤), Worst possible catastrophe (u⊥), Rational agent axioms, Utility assessment | Example questions: How can we determine an agent's utility function from its observed choices?; What does it mean to normalize utilities, and why are 0 and 1 commonly used as the scale endpoints?

children.title: 16.4 Multiattribute Utility Functions
children.abstract: This section introduces multi‑attribute utility theory as a way to evaluate decisions that involve several outcome attributes (e.g., cost, noise, safety). It explains how to represent attributes, define utility over attribute vectors, and use the concept of strict dominance to eliminate inferior alternatives before combining utilities. | Key concepts: Multi‑attribute utility theory, Attribute (X₁,…,Xₙ), Utility function, Attribute vector (x = ⟨x₁,…,xₙ⟩), Strict dominance, Dominance pruning, Ordering of attribute values, Decision under uncertainty | Example questions: How does strict dominance help reduce the number of alternatives in a multi‑attribute decision problem?; What is an attribute vector and how is it used in multi‑attribute utility functions?

children.title: 16.5 Decision Networks
children.abstract: This section introduces decision networks (also called influence diagrams) as a framework for rational decision‑making under uncertainty. It explains how decision networks extend Bayesian networks by adding decision and utility nodes, and discusses the role of utility independence and multiplicative utility functions in modeling preferences. | Key concepts: Decision network (influence diagram), Utility independence, Mutually utility independent (MUI), Multiplicative utility function, Additive utility function, Decision node, Chance (random) node, Utility (value) node, Bayesian network | Example questions: How do decision networks differ from standard Bayesian networks?; What is the significance of mutually utility independent attributes in constructing a utility function?

children.title: 16.6 The Value of Information
children.abstract: Section 16.6 explains why decision makers rarely have all relevant data up front and introduces the concept of the Value of Information (VoI) as a way to quantify the benefit of acquiring additional evidence before acting. It shows how to compute VoI using decision‑network evaluation, distinguishing between perfect and imperfect information and linking the calculation to expected utility. | Key concepts: Value of Information (VoI), Perfect Information, Imperfect Information, Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI), Decision Network, Decision Node, Chance Node, Utility Node, Expected Utility, Bayesian Inference | Example questions: How do you calculate the value of perfect information in a decision network?; Why is it useful to consider the value of information when planning which diagnostic tests to order?

children.title: 16.7 Decision-Theoretic Expert Systems
children.abstract: This section explains how decision‑theoretic principles are applied to expert systems, covering the use of value‑of‑information analysis, conditional planning, and utility‑based question ordering to improve decision quality and human interaction. It also introduces the roles of decision makers and decision analysts in the decision‑analysis process that underlies these systems. | Key concepts: Decision‑theoretic expert system, Value of information (VOI), Myopic (greedy) decision agent, Conditional plan, Utility (total utility, human utility), Decision analysis, Decision maker, Decision analyst, Preference elicitation, Question ordering for maximum utility | Example questions: How does a decision‑theoretic expert system decide whether to ask for more evidence before taking an action?; What are the roles of the decision maker and decision analyst in decision analysis for expert systems?

children.title: 16.8 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes how probability theory, utility theory, and decision theory combine to enable rational agents to make optimal choices. It covers utility functions, multi‑attribute utilities, stochastic dominance, decision networks, and the value of information for guiding decisions under uncertainty. | Key concepts: Probability theory, Utility theory, Decision theory, Rational agent, Multi‑attribute utility, Stochastic dominance, Decision networks, Value of information, Expected utility | Example questions: How does decision theory combine probability and utility to determine the best action for an agent?; What is stochastic dominance and how can it be used when precise utility values are unavailable?

children.title: 17 Making Complex Decisions
children.abstract: This section introduces sequential decision problems, where an agent must choose actions over time in a stochastic and possibly partially observable environment. It explains how to model and solve these problems for optimal behavior, and extends the discussion to multi‑agent settings and game‑theoretic considerations. | Key concepts: Sequential decision problem, Stochastic environment, Utility (reward) function, Dynamic programming / Bellman equation, Partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), Decision network, Dynamic Bayesian network, Game theory, Mixed (randomized) strategies, Multi‑agent coordination | Example questions: How do we model and compute optimal actions when an agent must make a series of decisions under uncertainty?; What techniques are used to handle decision making in partially observable or multi‑agent environments?

children.title: 17.1 Sequential Decision Problems
children.abstract: Section 17.1 introduces sequential decision problems, where an agent must choose actions over multiple time steps in a stochastic environment, and its overall utility depends on the entire action sequence. It defines the formal model (states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and horizon) and contrasts it with one‑shot decision problems, setting the stage for optimal planning under uncertainty. | Key concepts: Sequential decision problem, Markov decision process (MDP), State space, Action space, Transition probability, Reward function, Policy, Horizon (finite vs. infinite), Utility of a decision sequence, Stochastic environment | Example questions: What is the formal definition of a sequential decision problem and how does it differ from a one‑shot decision problem?; How are states, actions, transition probabilities, and rewards combined to model an agent’s decision making over time?

children.title: 17.2 Value Iteration
children.abstract: This section introduces the value‑iteration algorithm for solving Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). It explains how the Bellman equation relates a state's utility to its immediate reward and the discounted utilities of successor states, and shows how iteratively applying this equation converges to the optimal utilities and policy. | Key concepts: Value Iteration, Bellman Equation, Utility (U(s)), Discount factor (γ), Markov Decision Process (MDP), Optimal policy, State transition probabilities (P(s'|s,a)), Max operator in Bellman update, Convergence of iterative updates | Example questions: How does the Bellman equation define the utility of a state in a Markov Decision Process?; What steps does the value‑iteration algorithm follow to compute the optimal policy for an MDP?

children.title: 17.3 Policy Iteration
children.abstract: This section explains the policy‑iteration algorithm for solving Markov decision processes. It details the two alternating steps—policy evaluation (computing state utilities for a fixed policy) and policy improvement (deriving a new MEU policy via one‑step look‑ahead)—and shows why the process converges to an optimal policy in a finite number of iterations. | Key concepts: Policy Iteration, Policy Evaluation, Policy Improvement, MEU (Maximum Expected Utility) Policy, Bellman Equation, Utility Function (Uπ), Discount Factor (γ), Convergence and Fixed Point, Finite State Space, Termination Criterion | Example questions: What are the steps of the policy‑iteration algorithm and how does each step work?; Why does policy iteration always converge to an optimal policy for a finite MDP?

children.title: 17.4 Partially Observable MDPs
children.abstract: This section introduces Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), explaining how they extend ordinary MDPs to settings where the agent cannot directly observe the true state. It discusses why optimal policies must depend on the agent’s knowledge (belief) about the state and highlights the added complexity compared to fully observable MDPs. | Key concepts: POMDP (Partially Observable Markov Decision Process), Belief state, Observation model, Transition model, Policy (mapping from belief to action), Utility (expected cumulative reward), Partial observability, Markov assumption, Optimal policy under uncertainty | Example questions: How does a POMDP differ from a regular MDP, and why can’t we use the same policy representation?; What is a belief state in a POMDP and how is it used to choose actions?

children.title: 17.5 Decisions with Multiple Agents: Game Theory
children.abstract: Section 17.5 introduces game theory as the framework for making decisions when multiple rational agents interact, highlighting how each agent’s uncertainty stems from the choices of others. It covers basic concepts such as strategic form and extensive‑form representations, solution concepts like Nash equilibrium and dominant strategies, and distinguishes between cooperative and non‑cooperative settings. | Key concepts: Game Theory, Strategic (Normal) Form, Extensive Form, Nash Equilibrium, Dominant Strategy, Mixed Strategy, Payoff Matrix, Cooperative vs. Non‑cooperative Games, Rational Agent | Example questions: How does a Nash equilibrium differ from a dominant‑strategy solution in a game?; What are the main differences between the strategic (normal) form and the extensive form of a game?

children.title: 17.6 Mechanism Design
children.abstract: This section introduces mechanism design, the inverse problem of game theory where we construct games (or mechanisms) so that rational behavior by self‑interested agents leads to outcomes that maximize a desired global objective. It outlines the components of a mechanism—strategy language, a central authority, and an outcome rule—and illustrates the concept with real‑world examples such as auctions, network routing, and assignment problems. | Key concepts: Mechanism design, Inverse game theory, Strategy space, Center (or mechanism designer), Outcome rule, Global utility function, Incentive compatibility, Auction theory, Social welfare maximization, Strategic equilibrium | Example questions: How does mechanism design differ from traditional game analysis, and what are its main components?; What is an outcome rule in a mechanism, and why is incentive compatibility important for achieving the desired global utility?

children.title: 17.7 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: The section first explains why the Vickrey‑Clarke‑Groves (VCG) mechanism is truth‑revealing, showing that reporting one’s true utility is a dominant strategy. It then summarizes the chapter’s main ideas on making decisions under uncertainty, focusing on Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), their components (transition model, reward function, discounting), and the notion of an optimal policy that maximizes expected utility. | Key concepts: Vickrey‑Clarke‑Groves (VCG) mechanism, Truth‑revealing / incentive compatibility, Dominant strategy, Utility (true vs. reported), Markov Decision Process (MDP), Transition model, Reward function, Discount factor, Policy, Optimal policy | Example questions: Why does the VCG mechanism guarantee that agents will report their true valuations?; What are the key components of an MDP and how do they determine an optimal policy?

chapters.title: V: Learning
chapters.abstract: This section introduces the concept of learning in artificial agents, explaining why agents need to acquire knowledge from experience rather than being fully pre‑programmed. It outlines the motivations for learning, surveys major forms of learning, and previews specific learning methods such as decision‑tree learning, linear and nonlinear models, non‑parametric approaches, support vector machines, and model ensembles. | Key concepts: Learning agent, Input–output pairs, Decision‑tree learning, Linear models, Neural networks, Non‑parametric models, Support vector machines (SVMs), Ensembles of models, Adaptation to changing environments, Uncertain knowledge and reasoning | Example questions: Why is it important for an AI agent to learn from examples instead of having all behavior hard‑coded?; What are the main categories of learning methods discussed in this section, and how do decision trees differ from neural networks?

children.title: 18 Learning from Examples
children.abstract: This section introduces the concept of learning from examples, explaining why agents need to learn from data rather than being fully programmed. It outlines the motivations for learning, surveys major forms of learning, and previews specific techniques such as decision‑tree learning, linear and nonlinear models, non‑parametric methods, support vector machines, and ensemble approaches. | Key concepts: Learning from examples, Agent performance improvement, Input–output pairs, Decision‑tree learning, Linear models, Neural networks (nonlinear models), Non‑parametric models, Support vector machines, Ensemble methods, Generalization | Example questions: Why do we need learning algorithms for agents instead of hard‑coding all possible behaviors?; What are the main categories of models used for learning from input‑output examples?

children.title: 18.1 Forms of Learning
children.abstract: Section 18.1 introduces the motivation for machine learning by defining what it means for an agent to learn and explaining why designers rely on learning algorithms instead of hard‑coding solutions. It outlines three core reasons for learning—unforeseen situations, changing environments, and tasks that are hard to program—and sets the stage for the various learning paradigms discussed later in the chapter. | Key concepts: Agent learning, Performance improvement, Input–output pairs, Generalization to new inputs, Unforeseen situations, Non‑stationary environments, Learning as a solution to hard‑to‑program tasks, Decision‑tree learning, Linear and nonlinear models, Ensemble methods | Example questions: Why do we need learning algorithms instead of just programming all possible behaviors into an agent?; What are the main reasons that motivate the use of learning in AI systems according to Section 18.1?

children.title: 18.2 Supervised Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces supervised learning as a paradigm where an agent learns a mapping from inputs to outputs using labeled example pairs provided by a teacher. It contrasts supervised learning with reinforcement learning and mentions related approaches such as semi‑supervised learning, highlighting practical challenges like noisy or inaccurate labels. | Key concepts: Supervised Learning, Input–Output Pairs, Teacher (Label Provider), Function Approximation, Reinforcement Learning, Semi‑Supervised Learning, Labeled vs. Unlabeled Data, Noisy Labels, Training Examples, Mapping Function | Example questions: How does supervised learning differ from reinforcement learning in terms of the information the agent receives?; What challenges arise when the labels in a supervised learning dataset are noisy or partially incorrect?

children.title: 18.3 Learning Decision Trees
children.abstract: This section explains how decision‑tree learning fits within the broader framework of supervised learning, emphasizing the role of the hypothesis space, the notion of realizability, and Bayesian selection of hypotheses. It also discusses the trade‑off between expressive hypothesis spaces and computational feasibility, illustrating why simpler models are often preferred. | Key concepts: Hypothesis space (H), Realizable learning problem, Bayesian hypothesis selection (MAP), Prior probability P(h), Likelihood P(data|h), Expressiveness vs. computational complexity, Undecidability of learning arbitrary Turing machines, Model simplicity (Occam’s razor), Degree of polynomial hypotheses | Example questions: What does it mean for a learning problem to be realizable, and how does that affect hypothesis selection?; Why do we prefer simpler hypothesis spaces over something as expressive as all Turing machines when learning decision trees?

children.title: 18.4 Evaluating and Choosing the Best Hypothesis
children.abstract: This section explains how to evaluate and select the hypothesis that will perform best on future data by introducing the stationarity (i.i.d.) assumption, defining error rate as a measure of fit, and describing the holdout (cross‑validation) method for estimating generalization performance. | Key concepts: Stationarity assumption, Independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) examples, Error rate, Generalization, Holdout cross‑validation, Training set, Test set, Future data distribution | Example questions: How does the i.i.d. (stationarity) assumption help us relate past training data to future examples?; Why is holdout cross‑validation needed instead of just measuring error on the training set?

children.title: 18.5 The Theory of Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces the formal theory of learning by defining a total cost that combines empirical loss with hypothesis complexity, using a regularization parameter λ to balance the two. It explains regularization, how to choose loss and complexity measures, and discusses related techniques such as feature selection and χ² pruning, as well as the idea of measuring both loss and complexity in bits (MDL). | Key concepts: Total Cost (Cost(h) = EmpLoss(h) + λ·Complexity(h)), Regularization, Regularization Parameter (λ), Loss Function, Complexity Measure / Regularization Function, Feature Selection, χ² Pruning, Minimum Description Length (MDL), Cross‑validation for λ selection | Example questions: How does the regularization parameter λ affect the trade‑off between fitting the training data and keeping the model simple?; What is the difference between regularization and feature selection, and how can χ² pruning be used in feature selection?
