children.title: 18.7 Artificial Neural Networks
children.abstract: Section 18.7 introduces artificial neural networks by first revisiting logistic regression, showing its weight‑update rule derived from the logistic function’s derivative, and comparing its convergence behavior on linearly separable versus noisy, non‑separable data. It then connects these learning concepts to modeling brain activity, highlighting the reciprocal influence between neuroscience and machine‑learning techniques. | Key concepts: Logistic regression, Logistic function derivative (g′(z) = g(z)(1‑g(z))), Weight update rule for logistic regression, Squared error loss, Convergence behavior on separable vs. non‑separable data, Applications of logistic regression (medicine, marketing, credit scoring, etc.), Artificial neural networks (ANNs), Relationship between neural models and neuroscience | Example questions: How is the weight update formula for logistic regression derived from the logistic function’s derivative?; Why does logistic regression converge faster than a linear threshold classifier on noisy, non‑separable data?

children.title: 18.8 Nonparametric Models
children.abstract: This section introduces non‑parametric learning models, contrasting them with parametric approaches, and discusses how neural network architectures can be adapted by pruning (e.g., Optimal Brain Damage) or growing (e.g., the Tiling algorithm). It emphasizes the need for validation when selecting network size and topology. | Key concepts: Parametric vs. non‑parametric models, Optimal Brain Damage (pruning connections), Tiling algorithm (incremental network growth), Network architecture selection, Cross‑validation for model selection, Fully‑connected vs. sparsely‑connected networks, Unit/connection removal criteria, Training‑set vs. validation‑set usage | Example questions: How does the Optimal Brain Damage algorithm prune a neural network, and why is cross‑validation important when doing so?; What is the Tiling algorithm and how does it differ from simply adding more hidden units to a neural network?

children.title: 18.9 Support Vector Machines
children.abstract: This section introduces Support Vector Machines (SVMs) as a versatile, off‑the‑shelf supervised learning method. It explains the three main attractions of SVMs—maximum‑margin separation, the kernel trick that enables linear separators in high‑dimensional feature spaces, and their non‑parametric nature that often leads to sparse models composed of support vectors. | Key concepts: Maximum margin separator, Hyperplane, Kernel trick, Linear separability, Non‑parametric model, Support vectors, Feature space transformation, Regularization parameter (C), Soft‑margin SVM | Example questions: Why do SVMs tend to generalize better than other linear classifiers?; How does the kernel trick allow an SVM to create nonlinear decision boundaries?

children.title: 18.10 Ensemble Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces ensemble learning, explaining how combining multiple hypotheses—such as decision trees generated during cross‑validation—can improve prediction accuracy compared to using a single model. It outlines the basic idea of forming an ensemble, aggregating their votes, and hints at the motivations behind methods like bagging and boosting. | Key concepts: Ensemble Learning, Hypothesis Space, Voting/Aggregation, Decision Tree, Cross‑validation, Bagging, Boosting, Random Forest, Model Diversity, Bias‑Variance Tradeoff | Example questions: Why does combining several decision trees usually give better classification performance than a single tree?; What is the main idea behind ensemble learning and how are the predictions of individual models combined?

children.title: 18.11 Practical Machine Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces online (practical) machine learning, focusing on algorithms that make predictions sequentially and adapt to changing data by minimizing regret relative to a set of expert advisors. It explains how the choice of the learning rate parameter β influences the trade‑off between responsiveness to expert changes and early‑stage penalties, and describes the concept of no‑regret learning and its usefulness for large, continuously growing datasets. | Key concepts: Online learning, Regret bound, No‑regret learning, Expert advice algorithm, Learning rate parameter (β), M* (mistakes of the best expert), Adaptive weighting of experts, Incremental model updating, Trade‑off between responsiveness and early‑stage error | Example questions: How does the choice of the β parameter affect the regret bound in the expert‑advice online learning algorithm?; What is no‑regret learning and why is it useful for continuously growing datasets like a web‑image database?

children.title: 18.12 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes the key ideas from the chapter on inductive learning, covering supervised learning (classification and regression), the role of hypothesis selection (Ockham’s razor), decision‑tree learning with information‑gain heuristics, learning curves, and practical guidelines for choosing learning algorithms such as decision trees, non‑parametric methods, and support vector machines. | Key concepts: Supervised learning, Classification vs. regression, Inductive learning and hypothesis selection, Ockham’s razor, Decision trees, Information‑gain heuristic, Learning curve, Non‑parametric methods, Support vector machines | Example questions: What are the main differences between classification and regression in supervised learning?; When should I prefer decision trees over support vector machines for a new dataset?

children.title: 19 Knowledge in Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces how prior knowledge can be incorporated into learning by representing hypotheses, examples, and classifications as first‑order logical sentences. It shows how logical inference enables incremental hypothesis construction and leverages existing knowledge to improve classification. | Key concepts: Prior knowledge, First‑order logical theory, Logical formulation of learning, Hypothesis space, Inductive learning, Incremental hypothesis construction, Logical inference, Example description, Classification sentence, Knowledge representation | Example questions: How can existing logical knowledge be used to guide the learning process?; What does it mean to represent hypotheses and examples as first‑order logical sentences?

children.title: 19.1 ALogical Formulation of Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces a logical approach to machine learning, where hypotheses, examples, and classifications are expressed as first‑order logical sentences. It shows how prior knowledge encoded in logical theories can be integrated into the learning process, enabling incremental hypothesis construction and inference‑driven classification. | Key concepts: Logical hypothesis space, First‑order logical sentences, Prior knowledge representation, Inductive learning as logical inference, Incremental hypothesis construction, Example description and classification sentences, Logical entailment for classification, Integration of knowledge representation and learning | Example questions: How does representing hypotheses as logical sentences allow prior knowledge to be used in learning?; What is the role of logical inference in classifying new examples in the logical formulation of learning?

children.title: 19.2 Knowledge in Learning
children.abstract: This section explains how prior knowledge influences inductive learning by formalizing the relationship between hypotheses, example descriptions, and classifications as an entailment constraint. It contrasts pure, knowledge‑free learning with modern knowledge‑based approaches that start with background knowledge and apply principles like Ockham’s razor to prefer simpler, consistent hypotheses. | Key concepts: Entailment constraint, Hypothesis space, Prior/background knowledge, Inductive learning, Ockham’s razor, Consistent hypothesis, Cumulative learning process, Knowledge‑based learning, Logical entailment (|=), Decision tree as logical formula | Example questions: How does prior knowledge change the way we formulate the learning problem in inductive learning?; What is an entailment constraint and why is it important for selecting consistent hypotheses?

children.title: 19.3 Explanation-Based Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces Explanation‑Based Learning (EBL), a technique that uses existing domain knowledge to derive general rules from single observations, thereby shrinking the hypothesis space and simplifying learning. It illustrates EBL with a calculus example, showing how a system can learn the differentiation rule for X² by analyzing a single proof and then applying the derived rule to future problems. | Key concepts: Explanation‑Based Learning (EBL), Prior knowledge / background knowledge, Hypothesis space reduction, Inductive Logic Programming (ILP), First‑order logic representation, Generalization from a single example, Proof steps and dead‑end branches, Differentiation rule (Derivative(X², X) = 2X), Knowledge base (KB) | Example questions: How does Explanation‑Based Learning use prior knowledge to reduce the number of hypotheses that need to be considered?; In the calculus example, how does the system extract a general differentiation rule from a single proof of X²?

children.title: 19.4 Learning Using Relevance Information
children.abstract: Section 19.4 explains how learning systems can exploit relevance information—knowledge about which facts or features are pertinent to a task—to guide the acquisition of useful rules and improve efficiency. It shows how background knowledge (e.g., nationality implies language) can be formalized in first‑order logic to focus learning on the most relevant aspects of examples, thereby reducing average‑case complexity. | Key concepts: Explanation‑Based Learning (EBL), Relevance information, Background knowledge, First‑order logic representation, Generalization, Average‑case complexity, PAC learning assumption, Empirical rule selection, Efficiency of knowledge bases, Recursive rules | Example questions: How does relevance information help an EBL system choose which rules to learn?; Why is background knowledge expressed in first‑order logic important for learning efficient generalizations?

children.title: 19.5 Inductive Logic Programming
children.abstract: This section introduces Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) as a method that combines inductive learning with first‑order logic representations, explaining why ILP is valuable, how it formulates the knowledge‑based induction problem using logical entailment, and illustrating the approach with a family‑relationship learning example. | Key concepts: Inductive Logic Programming (ILP), First‑order logic representations, Knowledge‑based induction problem, Entailment constraint (Background ∧ Hypothesis ∧ Descriptions ⊨ Classifications), Background knowledge, Hypothesis space, Attribute‑based vs relational learning, Explainable hypotheses, Family relationship learning example | Example questions: How does Inductive Logic Programming formulate the learning problem using logical entailment?; Why is ILP preferred over attribute‑based methods for domains like protein structure prediction?

children.title: 19.6 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section reviews the practical impact of Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) in scientific discovery, highlighting notable case studies where ILP systems such as PROGOL have uncovered novel biological rules, outperformed traditional methods on challenging datasets, and even enabled autonomous experimental design. It also emphasizes the importance of relational representation and background knowledge for ILP’s success and interpretability. | Key concepts: Inductive Logic Programming (ILP), PROGOL, Protein folding rule discovery, Mutagenicity prediction of nitroaromatic compounds, Experiment design for autonomous scientific robots, Background knowledge in ILP, Interpretability of learned rules, Comparison with linear regression, neural networks, decision trees | Example questions: How has ILP been used to discover new rules in molecular biology, and what examples illustrate its success?; In what situations does ILP outperform traditional machine‑learning methods like linear regression or neural networks?

children.title: 20 Learning Probabilistic Models
children.abstract: This section introduces learning probabilistic models as a form of uncertain reasoning, framing learning itself as Bayesian inference over data and hypotheses. It explains how agents can infer the underlying probabilistic theory of a domain (e.g., Bayesian networks) from observations, handling noise, over‑fitting, and prediction uncertainty. | Key concepts: Probabilistic learning, Bayesian inference, Statistical learning, Data (evidence) vs. hypotheses (theories), Bayesian networks, Over‑fitting, Noise handling, Predictive inference, Prior and posterior distributions, Model selection | Example questions: How does a Bayesian approach help an agent learn a probabilistic model from noisy observations?; What is the difference between data and hypotheses in the context of statistical learning?

children.title: 20.1 Statistical Learning
children.abstract: Section 20.1 introduces statistical learning as probabilistic inference, showing how agents can learn uncertain models of the world from data. It emphasizes the Bayesian perspective, illustrating how hypotheses about probability distributions (e.g., Bayesian networks) are updated with evidence to handle noise, over‑fitting, and optimal prediction. | Key concepts: Statistical learning, Probabilistic inference, Bayesian learning, Hypotheses (probabilistic theories), Data as evidence, Noise and over‑fitting, Bayesian networks, Posterior distribution, Prior probability, Predictive inference | Example questions: How does a Bayesian approach help a learning agent deal with noisy observations and avoid over‑fitting?; What is the role of data and hypotheses in statistical learning, and how are they combined using probabilistic inference?

children.title: 20.2 Learning with Complete Data
children.abstract: Section 20.2 introduces learning probabilistic models when the dataset is complete, focusing on maximum‑likelihood parameter estimation for discrete distributions (e.g., estimating the cherry‑lime candy proportion). It also touches on learning model structure and non‑parametric density estimation. | Key concepts: Complete data, Maximum‑likelihood estimation (MLE), Parameter learning, Discrete probability model, Hypothesis (hθ), Likelihood function, Bayesian network (single‑node example), Structure learning (brief overview), Non‑parametric density estimation | Example questions: How do I compute the maximum‑likelihood estimate of a Bernoulli parameter when I have counts of successes and failures?; What does 'complete data' mean in the context of learning probabilistic models, and why does it simplify parameter estimation?

children.title: 20.3 Learning with Hidden Variables: The EM Algorithm
children.abstract: Section 20.3 introduces learning when some variables are hidden (latent) and explains why the Expectation‑Maximization (EM) algorithm is needed to estimate model parameters in such cases. It illustrates the impact of hidden variables on model complexity using a diagnostic example and sets up the EM framework for handling incomplete data. | Key concepts: Hidden (latent) variables, Expectation‑Maximization (EM) algorithm, Incomplete / missing data, E‑step (expectation step), M‑step (maximization step), Likelihood function, Parameter estimation, Model complexity and parameter count, Convergence of EM | Example questions: How does the EM algorithm handle parameters when some variables in my data are unobserved?; Why does removing a hidden variable from a Bayesian network dramatically increase the number of parameters?

children.title: 20.4 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: Section 20.4 summarizes the core ideas of statistical learning presented in the chapter, covering Bayesian and MAP learning, maximum‑likelihood estimation, the EM algorithm for hidden variables, structure learning for Bayesian networks, and non‑parametric approaches such as nearest‑neighbors and kernel methods. It highlights the trade‑offs between model complexity and fit, and notes the computational challenges of full Bayesian inference. | Key concepts: Bayesian learning, Maximum a posteriori (MAP) learning, Maximum‑likelihood estimation, Expectation‑Maximization (EM) algorithm, Structure learning for Bayesian networks, Model selection, Non‑parametric models, Nearest‑neighbors methods, Kernel methods | Example questions: How does MAP learning differ from full Bayesian learning and when is it more practical?; What algorithm can be used to estimate parameters when some variables are hidden, and what are typical applications of this algorithm?

children.title: 21 Reinforcement Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces reinforcement learning, explaining how an agent can learn appropriate actions through rewards and punishments rather than explicit labeled examples. It connects the concept of reward to optimal policies in Markov decision processes and contrasts it with supervised learning approaches. | Key concepts: Reinforcement Learning, Reward (Positive Reinforcement), Punishment (Negative Reinforcement), Agent, Policy, Optimal Policy, Markov Decision Process (MDP), Transition Model, Supervised Learning (contrast), Reinforcement Signal | Example questions: How does reinforcement learning differ from supervised learning when training an agent to play chess?; What role does a reward play in defining an optimal policy within a Markov decision process?

children.title: 21.1 Introduction
children.abstract: This section introduces reinforcement learning, explaining how agents can learn optimal behavior from rewards and punishments rather than labeled examples. It contrasts reinforcement learning with supervised learning, discusses the role of reward signals (including delayed rewards), and connects the concept to Markov decision processes and optimal policies. | Key concepts: Reinforcement Learning, Reward (Positive Reinforcement), Punishment (Negative Reinforcement), Supervised Learning, Transition Model, Markov Decision Process (MDP), Optimal Policy, Agent, Hardwired Reward Recognition, Feedback | Example questions: How does reinforcement learning differ from supervised learning in terms of the feedback an agent receives?; What is an optimal policy in a Markov decision process and how is it related to rewards?

children.title: 21.2 Passive Reinforcement Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces passive reinforcement learning, where an agent follows a fixed policy and learns the utility of each state solely from experience, without knowing the transition probabilities or reward function. It explains how the agent gathers data through trials in a fully observable environment and uses that data to evaluate the policy’s performance. | Key concepts: Passive reinforcement learning, Policy (π), Utility function Uπ(s), Transition model P(s' | s, a), Reward function R(s), Fully observable environment, Policy evaluation, Trial (episode), State‑based representation, Discount factor (γ) | Example questions: How can an agent estimate the utility of states when it doesn’t know the transition model or reward function?; What is the difference between passive reinforcement learning and the policy evaluation step in policy iteration?

children.title: 21.3 Active Reinforcement Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces active reinforcement learning, explaining how an agent must learn a full model of action outcomes and use the Bellman equations to compute optimal utilities. It highlights the necessity of exploration—rather than always following the current optimal policy—to avoid converging on suboptimal behaviors. | Key concepts: Active Reinforcement Learning, Passive Learning Agent, Adaptive Dynamic Programming (ADP), Bellman Equation, Utility Function, Optimal Policy, Exploration vs. Exploitation, Value Iteration, Policy Iteration | Example questions: Why does an active RL agent need to explore instead of always executing the policy it currently thinks is optimal?; How are the Bellman equations used in active reinforcement learning to compute the utility of states?

children.title: 21.4 Generalization in Reinforcement Learning
children.abstract: This section compares model‑based (e.g., ADP) and model‑free (e.g., Q‑learning, SARSA) reinforcement‑learning approaches, emphasizing how learning a model can improve generalization and speed of convergence, especially as state spaces grow beyond what tabular representations can handle. It also discusses the trade‑offs between knowledge‑based (model‑centric) representations and direct action‑value learning, and introduces the need for function approximation to achieve scalability. | Key concepts: Q‑learning, SARSA, Adaptive Dynamic Programming (ADP), Model‑based reinforcement learning, Model‑free reinforcement learning, Utility function, Q‑function, Tabular representation, Function approximation / Generalization, Knowledge‑based approach | Example questions: Why do model‑based methods like ADP often learn faster than model‑free methods such as Q‑learning in larger state spaces?; What are the limitations of using a tabular Q‑function, and how does function approximation address them?

children.title: 21.5 Policy Search
children.abstract: Section 21.5 introduces policy search as a reinforcement‑learning approach that directly optimizes a parameterized policy rather than estimating value functions. It explains how policies can be represented (e.g., via parameterized Q‑functions or neural networks), contrasts policy search with Q‑learning, and highlights that the goal is to adjust the parameters to improve actual performance, not necessarily to approximate the optimal Q‑function. | Key concepts: Policy search, Parameterized policy (π), Q‑function approximation (ĤQθ), Policy parameter vector (θ), Performance-driven optimization, Difference between policy search and Q‑learning, Function approximation (linear, neural network), Policy improvement loop | Example questions: How does policy search differ from Q‑learning when using function approximation?; What does it mean to represent a policy with a parameterized Q‑function and how are the parameters updated?

children.title: 21.6 Applications of Reinforcement Learning
children.abstract: This section introduces large‑scale applications of reinforcement learning, focusing on how techniques like correlated sampling and the PEGASUS policy‑search algorithm enable reliable evaluation of policies, and it surveys early successes in game playing (e.g., Samuel’s checkers program) and robotics where the environment model may be unknown. | Key concepts: Correlated sampling, PEGASUS algorithm, Policy search, Reinforcement learning in game playing, Reinforcement learning in robotics, Utility function learning, Simulation-based evaluation, Complexity of policy space vs. domain complexity, Arthur Samuel's checkers program | Example questions: How does the PEGASUS algorithm use correlated sampling to evaluate reinforcement‑learning policies?; What were the first major reinforcement‑learning applications in games, and how did Samuel’s checkers program work?

children.title: 21.7 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: Section 21.7 summarizes the main ideas of reinforcement learning covered in Chapter V, highlighting the three major agent designs (model‑based, model‑free, reflex), the three utility‑learning approaches (direct estimation, adaptive dynamic programming, temporal‑difference), and the ways Q‑functions can be learned. It also touches on the exploration‑exploitation trade‑off that arises when an agent must act while it is still learning. | Key concepts: Model‑based design, Model‑free design, Reflex (policy) design, Direct utility estimation, Adaptive Dynamic Programming (ADP), Temporal‑Difference (TD) learning, Q‑learning, Exploration‑exploitation trade‑off, Utility function U, Policy π | Example questions: What are the three main approaches for learning utilities in reinforcement learning?; How does Q‑learning differ from ADP‑based methods in terms of model requirements?

chapters.title: VI: Communicating, perceiving, and acting
chapters.abstract: This section introduces Natural Language Processing (NLP) as a means for artificial agents to understand and use human language, focusing on knowledge acquisition from text. It explains the role of language models—probabilistic models that predict language expressions—and connects them to core NLP tasks such as text classification, information retrieval, and information extraction. | Key concepts: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Language Model, Knowledge Acquisition, Text Classification, Information Retrieval, Information Extraction, Formal Language, Turing Test, Ambiguity in Language, Probability Distribution of Language | Example questions: Why are language models important for an AI system that needs to learn from web text?; What are the main NLP tasks discussed in this section and how do they relate to knowledge acquisition?

children.title: 22 Natural Language Processing
children.abstract: This section introduces Natural Language Processing (NLP) as the means for computer agents to understand and use human language, emphasizing its role in communication with users and in extracting knowledge from the massive amount of text on the Web. It outlines core NLP tasks—text classification, information retrieval, and information extraction—and explains that language models, which assign probabilities to language expressions, are the common foundation for tackling these tasks. | Key concepts: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Turing Test, Language Model, Text Classification, Information Retrieval, Information Extraction, Knowledge Acquisition, Formal Language, Ambiguity in Natural Language | Example questions: Why are language models essential for tasks like text classification and information retrieval?; What is the difference between a formal language (e.g., Python) and natural language in the context of language modeling?

children.title: 22.1 Language Models
children.abstract: This section introduces natural language processing and the role of language models in enabling computers to understand and generate human language. It explains why language capability is essential for communication and knowledge acquisition, contrasts natural language with formal programming languages, and outlines common NLP tasks such as text classification, information retrieval, and information extraction. | Key concepts: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Language Model, Formal Language, Text Classification, Information Retrieval, Information Extraction, Probability Distribution of Language, Knowledge Acquisition, Turing Test | Example questions: Why are language models important for AI agents that need to acquire knowledge from the web?; How do language models differ between natural languages and formal programming languages?

children.title: 22.2 Text Classification
children.abstract: Section 22.2 introduces text classification, explaining how to assign a document to one of several predefined categories (e.g., spam vs. ham, sentiment, language or genre). It discusses treating classification as a supervised learning problem, illustrates typical training data, and highlights useful features such as word n‑grams and character‑level patterns. | Key concepts: Text classification / categorization, Supervised learning, Spam detection (spam vs. ham), Word n‑grams, Character‑level features, Training set (positive and negative examples), Feature selection, Genre classification, Sentiment analysis | Example questions: How can we use word n‑grams and character‑level features to build a spam‑filter classifier?; What is the difference between ‘spam’ and ‘ham’ in the context of text classification, and how is a supervised learning model trained for this task?

children.title: 22.3 Information Retrieval
children.abstract: This section introduces the fundamentals of Information Retrieval (IR), describing how IR systems organize a corpus of documents, interpret user queries, and retrieve relevant results. It also discusses a simple classification technique based on data compression and highlights the role of query languages and document granularity in building search engines. | Key concepts: Information Retrieval (IR), Corpus of documents, Query language, Compression‑based classification, Character n‑grams, Document granularity (paragraph, page, multi‑page), Relevance ranking, Search engine query example (e.g., "AI book"), Standard text classification corpora (20‑Newsgroups, Reuters‑10) | Example questions: How do compression algorithms like gzip help classify text in an information retrieval system?; What are the main components of an IR system and how does the query language affect search results?

children.title: 22.4 Information Extraction
children.abstract: This section explains how the ASKMSR system performs information extraction by rewriting natural‑language questions into multiple search‑engine queries, gathering short text snippets, extracting 1‑, 2‑, and 3‑grams, scoring them by frequency and query specificity, and then filtering the results by expected answer type (person, number, date, etc.) to produce concise answers. It also discusses how longer answers are assembled from shorter n‑gram pieces and notes ASKMSR’s strong performance at TREC. | Key concepts: ASKMSR, Query rewriting, n‑gram extraction, Weighting by query specificity, Answer‑type filtering, Pronoun reference limitation, TREC (Text Retrieval Evaluation Conference), Answer assembly from bigrams, Frequency scoring | Example questions: How does ASKMSR turn a natural‑language question into a search query?; What techniques does ASKMSR use to filter and rank candidate answer n‑grams?

children.title: 22.5 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section reviews the TEXTRUNNER system for open‑domain relation extraction using linear‑chain CRFs and a small set of linguistic templates. It highlights how a handful of generic templates cover most English relation expressions, reports the system’s precision/recall results on a massive web corpus, and connects these advances to the broader goal of machine reading. | Key concepts: TEXTRUNNER, Linear‑chain Conditional Random Field (CRF), Relation‑extraction templates, Precision, recall, and F1 score, Open‑domain information extraction, Domain‑independent feature set, Web‑scale corpus processing, Machine reading | Example questions: How does TEXTRUNNER use CRFs and templates to extract relational facts from unstructured text?; What are the reported precision, recall, and F1 scores for TEXTRUNNER on a large web corpus?

children.title: 23 Natural Language for Communication
children.abstract: This section introduces natural language as a means of communication for both humans and computer agents, emphasizing the need for richer linguistic models beyond simple n‑gram statistics. It covers phrase‑structure grammars, lexical categories, and how generalization helps mitigate data sparsity in language modeling, setting the stage for deeper semantic and translation tasks. | Key concepts: Natural language communication, Phrase‑structure grammar, Lexical category (part of speech), n‑gram language model, Data sparsity, Generalization in language modeling, Adjective‑noun ordering, Machine translation, Speech recognition | Example questions: Why are n‑gram models insufficient for capturing the structure of natural language, and how do phrase‑structure grammars help?; What is data sparsity in language modeling, and how does generalizing lexical categories reduce its impact?

children.title: 23.1 Phrase Structure Grammars
children.abstract: Section 23.1 introduces phrase‑structure grammars as a way to overcome the data‑sparsity problems of n‑gram language models by capturing hierarchical syntactic regularities such as word order and lexical categories. It explains how generalizations about parts of speech (e.g., adjective‑noun order) can be encoded in grammar rules, laying the groundwork for richer semantic models used in translation and speech recognition. | Key concepts: Phrase‑structure grammar, Lexical category (part of speech), Data sparsity in n‑gram models, Generalization through syntactic rules, Adjective‑noun ordering, Grammar rules / productions, Hierarchical sentence structure, Application to machine translation, Application to speech recognition | Example questions: Why do n‑gram language models suffer from data sparsity and how do phrase‑structure grammars help?; What is a lexical category and how does it influence word order in English versus French?

children.title: 23.2 Syntactic Analysis (Parsing)
children.abstract: Section 23.2 introduces syntactic analysis, or parsing, as the process of mapping a sequence of words onto a phrase‑structure tree according to a grammar. It explains both top‑down and bottom‑up parsing strategies, highlights their inefficiencies due to redundant search, and illustrates these ideas with example sentences and a probabilistic parse tree. | Key concepts: Parsing, Top‑down parsing, Bottom‑up parsing, Phrase‑structure tree, Probabilistic grammar, Overgeneration, Undergeneration, Parse probability, Search space redundancy | Example questions: How do top‑down and bottom‑up parsing differ, and why can they be inefficient?; What does the probability of a parse tree represent in a probabilistic grammar?

children.title: 23.3 Augmented Grammars and Semantic Interpretation
children.abstract: This section explains how to enhance context‑free grammars with additional information—creating augmented grammars—to better capture lexical dependencies and global constraints such as expected sentence length. It introduces lexicalized probabilistic CFGs and discusses combining PCFGs with Markov models to improve semantic interpretation of sentences. | Key concepts: Augmented Grammars, Probabilistic Context‑Free Grammar (PCFG), Lexicalized PCFG, Markov Model (n‑gram language model), Geometric mean combination of probabilities, Sentence‑length bias in PCFGs, Soft global constraints, Lexical dependencies in parse trees, Semantic interpretation | Example questions: How do lexicalized PCFGs help capture the relationship between a verb and its distant noun arguments?; Why do standard PCFGs tend to favor short sentences, and how can augmented grammars address this bias?

children.title: 23.4 Machine Translation
children.abstract: This section introduces machine translation (MT) as the automatic conversion of text from a source language to a target language, outlines its historical roots and recent widespread adoption, and illustrates typical translation quality using a Google Translate example that shows both acceptable paraphrases and minor errors. It also briefly mentions the three traditional MT application categories, beginning with rough translation for quick gist extraction. | Key concepts: Machine Translation (MT), Source language, Target language, Rough translation, Post‑editing, Translation accuracy, Paraphrase vs. literal translation, Online MT tools (e.g., Google Translate), Error types (e.g., article omission), Historical development of MT | Example questions: What is machine translation and how has its usage changed over time?; What are the main types of machine‑translation applications and how do they differ in quality?

children.title: 23.5 Speech Recognition
children.abstract: This section explains how large‑scale statistical machine translation systems prepare bilingual corpora by segmenting text into sentences, aligning those sentences across languages, and then aligning phrases within sentences. It discusses practical techniques such as using punctuation cues, part‑of‑speech features, length‑based heuristics, Viterbi alignment, and lexical landmarks to achieve high accuracy. | Key concepts: Sentence segmentation, Sentence alignment, Phrase alignment, Statistical translation models, Viterbi algorithm for alignment, Part‑of‑speech features, Length‑based alignment heuristics, Lexical landmarks (numbers, dates, proper names), Parallel corpora | Example questions: How do translation systems decide whether a period marks the end of a sentence?; What methods are used to align sentences and phrases between English and French corpora?

children.title: 23.6 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section explains how speech recognition systems model the acoustic signal using phone models and hidden Markov models (HMMs), and how the model parameters are learned from speech corpora via the Expectation‑Maximization (EM) algorithm. It also discusses the role of pronunciation dictionaries and the benefits of speaker‑dependent training. | Key concepts: Pronunciation dictionary, Three‑state phone model, Hidden Markov Model (HMM), Expectation‑Maximization (EM) algorithm, Forward‑backward (smoothing) algorithm, Speech corpus with aligned transcripts, Speaker‑dependent training, Transition and sensor probabilities | Example questions: How are the transition and observation probabilities of a speech HMM estimated from raw audio data?; Why do high‑accuracy speech recognizers often train separate models for each speaker?

children.title: 24 Perception
children.abstract: This section introduces the concept of perception in artificial agents, explaining how sensors convert raw environmental data into usable information. It focuses on vision as a primary modality, describing sensor models, object models, and rendering models, and shows how Bayesian updating is used within partially observable environments. | Key concepts: Sensor, Perception modality, Active sensing, Sensor model (P(E|S)), Object model, Rendering model, Bayes' rule, POMDP (Partially Observable Markov Decision Process), Vision as a sensory channel | Example questions: How does an agent use Bayes' rule to update its belief about the world from visual sensor data?; What is the difference between an object model and a rendering model in computer vision?

children.title: 24.1 Image Formation
children.abstract: Section 24.1 discusses how visual information is used by agents, contrasting simple reflexive pathways (as in fruit flies) with more complex decision‑theoretic architectures. It outlines three major strategies for handling rich visual data—feature extraction, recognition, and reconstruction—and highlights the challenge of selecting relevant visual cues for action selection. | Key concepts: Decision‑theoretic agent, Reflex agent, Closed‑loop control, Feature extraction, Recognition, Reconstruction, Visual sensor bandwidth, Goal‑directed perception, Geometric world model | Example questions: What are the three main approaches to processing visual information in autonomous agents?; How do reflex‑based agents like fruit flies differ from decision‑theoretic agents in using visual data?

children.title: 24.2 Early Image-Processing Operations
children.abstract: This section explains how human color vision works and how it underpins early image‑processing operations. It introduces the principle of trichromacy, the modeling of surfaces and lights with red‑green‑blue (RGB) albedos and intensities, and the concept of color constancy that allows both humans and algorithms to perceive true surface colors under varying illumination. | Key concepts: Trichromacy, Spectral energy density, RGB (red‑green‑blue) color model, Lambert's cosine law, Albedo, Color constancy, Auto white balance, Human color receptors (cones), Illumination variation | Example questions: How does the principle of trichromacy allow a computer to represent any color using only red, green, and blue components?; What is color constancy and how is it implemented in simple image‑processing functions like auto white balance?

children.title: 24.3 Object Recognition by Appearance
children.abstract: This section explains how objects can be recognized by their visual appearance, focusing on image segmentation techniques that group pixels into regions using low‑level cues (brightness, color, texture) and graph‑based methods such as normalized cuts. It also discusses the limitations of purely low‑level segmentation and introduces the use of superpixels and high‑level object knowledge to improve boundary detection and object recognition. | Key concepts: Image segmentation, Graph partitioning, Normalized cut criterion, Superpixels, Over‑segmentation, Low‑level visual attributes (brightness, color, texture), High‑level object knowledge, Boundary contours, Appearance‑based object recognition | Example questions: How does the normalized cut algorithm use pixel similarity to segment an image?; Why are superpixels preferred over raw pixels when applying high‑level object knowledge for recognition?

children.title: 24.4 Reconstructing the 3D World
children.abstract: Section 24.4 explains how to transform 2‑D image data into a 3‑D representation of a scene. It covers the use of local feature descriptors (e.g., SIFT, HOG) for object detection, pose estimation, and the geometric principles (camera models, depth, stereo, structure‑from‑motion) that enable reconstruction of the world’s three‑dimensional structure. | Key concepts: SIFT (Scale‑Invariant Feature Transform), HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients), Feature descriptor, Pose estimation, Camera projection model, Depth map, Stereo vision, Structure‑from‑motion (SfM), Non‑maximum suppression, Object recognition pipeline | Example questions: How do SIFT and HOG features help in estimating the 3‑D pose of an object from a single image?; What are the main geometric steps required to reconstruct a depth map from a pair of stereo images?

children.title: 24.5 Object Recognition from Structural Information
children.abstract: This section explains how structural cues such as surface orientation (normal, slant, tilt) and geometric shape—both local (curvature) and global (invariance under rotations and translations)—are used for object recognition. It highlights the challenges of representing shape for diverse real‑world objects and introduces differential geometry as the framework for describing surface curvature. | Key concepts: Surface normal (n), Slant, Tilt, Shape invariance, Geometric transformations (rotation, translation), Local surface curvature, Differential geometry, Global vs. local shape representation, Object recognition cues (shape, color, texture), Manipulation planning (grasping based on shape) | Example questions: How do slant and tilt describe the orientation of a surface relative to the camera?; Why is curvature a useful descriptor for local shape when recognizing objects from visual input?

children.title: 24.6 Using Vision
children.abstract: Section 24.6 discusses how computer vision can be used to recognize human actions in video, focusing on practical detection methods such as fixed‑body‑configuration detectors and background subtraction. It also outlines potential applications of action‑aware vision systems, from smarter building design to interactive interfaces and surveillance. | Key concepts: Action detection, Fixed body configuration detector, False positive rate, Background subtraction, Foreground blob tracking, Human pose localization, Reactive interfaces, Surveillance applications, Video analytics | Example questions: How does background subtraction help in detecting people in a video stream?; What are the advantages of using a fixed body‑configuration detector for recognizing human actions?

children.title: 24.7 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section summarizes how robotic perception systems combine stereoscopic vision and inertial sensing to estimate pose, addressing challenges such as drift and the need for task‑specific information extraction. It highlights probabilistic fusion methods (e.g., Kalman filtering), the role of landmarks for correcting odometry errors, and the principle that vision should compute only the data required for a given task. | Key concepts: Stereoscopic camera systems, Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU), Visual odometry, Drift (cumulative positional error), Landmark‑based pose correction, Probabilistic evidence fusion, Kalman filtering, Task‑specific visual processing, Centimeter‑level positioning accuracy | Example questions: How do robots combine camera data with IMU measurements to reduce drift in visual odometry?; Why is it unnecessary for a robot’s vision system to reconstruct every detail of the scene for navigation tasks?

children.title: 25 Robotics
children.abstract: This section introduces the fundamentals of robotics, describing how robots combine effectors and sensors to interact with the physical world. It outlines the three main robot categories—manipulators, mobile robots, and unmanned ground/planetary rovers—and highlights typical applications for each type. | Key concepts: Effector, Sensor, Manipulator, Mobile robot, Unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), Planetary rover, Jointed arm, Wheel/leg locomotion, Industrial automation | Example questions: What are the primary components that allow a robot to perceive and act on its environment?; How do manipulators differ from mobile robots and what are some common uses for each?

children.title: 25.1 Introduction
children.abstract: This section introduces robotics by defining robots as physical agents equipped with effectors and sensors that interact with the environment. It outlines the three main robot categories—manipulators, mobile robots, and unmanned ground/planetary rovers—and gives examples of their applications. | Key concepts: Robot, Effector, Sensor, Manipulator, Mobile robot, Unmanned ground vehicle (UGV), Planetary rover, Jointed arm, Actuation, Perception | Example questions: What are the primary components that allow a robot to interact with its environment?; How do manipulators differ from mobile robots and what are some typical uses for each?

children.title: 25.2 Robot Hardware
children.abstract: This section introduces the physical components of robots, covering effectors, anchored manipulators, prosthetic devices, intelligent environments, and multibody (swarm) systems, and explains the challenges robots face in partially observable, stochastic, dynamic, and continuous real‑world settings. It also emphasizes the need for prior knowledge and the integration of perception, planning, and learning techniques to enable safe and efficient robot operation. | Key concepts: Effectors, Anchored manipulators, Prosthetic devices, Intelligent environments, Multibody (swarm) systems, Partial observability, Stochasticity, Dynamic continuous environments, Probabilistic state estimation, Reinforcement learning in robotics | Example questions: What hardware components differentiate mobile robots from anchored manipulators, and why does this affect their control strategies?; How do partial observability and stochasticity influence the design of learning algorithms for real‑world robots?

children.title: 25.3 Robotic Perception
children.abstract: This section introduces robotic perception, explaining how robots convert noisy sensor data into useful internal models of their environment. It discusses the challenges of partial observability and dynamics, and reviews the probabilistic state‑estimation tools—Kalman filters, particle filters, HMMs, and dynamic Bayes nets—that enable efficient belief updates while incorporating the robot’s own actions. | Key concepts: Robotic perception, Sensor noise, Partial observability, Kalman filter, Particle filter, Hidden Markov Model (HMM), Dynamic Bayes net, Belief state, State estimation, Internal representation | Example questions: How do robots use Kalman filters and particle filters to handle noisy sensor measurements?; What role do dynamic Bayes nets play in representing a robot’s perception and actions over time?

children.title: 25.4 Planning to Move
children.abstract: This section introduces the fundamentals of robot motion planning, covering how robots decide on movements for both point‑to‑point and compliant tasks. It explains the use of configuration space to represent robot states and outlines the two primary discrete approaches—cell decomposition and skeletonization—for solving continuous path‑planning problems under deterministic and perfectly localized conditions. | Key concepts: Point‑to‑point motion, Compliant motion, Configuration space (C‑space), Path planning, Cell decomposition, Skeletonization, Deterministic motion assumption, Exact robot localization | Example questions: What is the configuration space and why is it used for robot motion planning?; How do cell decomposition and skeletonization convert a continuous path‑planning problem into a graph‑search problem?

children.title: 25.5 Planning Uncertain Movements
children.abstract: This section compares two graph‑based methods for planning robot motions in uncertain or high‑dimensional configuration spaces: the Voronoi graph, which maximizes clearance but can be costly to compute and may produce long detours, and the probabilistic roadmap (PRM), which randomly samples free configurations to build a flexible graph that scales better to wide‑open and high‑dimensional spaces. It also discusses the theoretical incompleteness of PRMs and ways to improve their success probability. | Key concepts: Voronoi graph, Clearance, Configuration space, Probabilistic roadmap (PRM), Random sampling, Graph search, Incomplete planning, Probability of failure bound, Bidirectional expansion, High‑dimensional planning | Example questions: How does a probabilistic roadmap differ from a Voronoi graph for robot path planning?; Why might a Voronoi graph be unsuitable for high‑dimensional configuration spaces?

children.title: 25.6 Moving
children.abstract: Section 25.6 discusses the gap between high‑level motion planning and the physical act of moving a robot. It introduces dynamic state, differential equation models of robot dynamics, and explains why practical systems often separate planning (using kinematic models) from control (calculating forces to follow the planned path). | Key concepts: Dynamic state, Kinematic vs. dynamic models, Differential equations, Curse of dimensionality, Deterministic path planners, Inertia and force control, Worst‑case planning, Transition model, Robot actuation | Example questions: Why can’t a robot simply follow the geometric path produced by a deterministic planner?; What is the role of differential equations in modeling robot motion and how does dynamic state differ from kinematic state?

children.title: 25.7 Robotic Software Architectures
children.abstract: This section introduces robotic software architectures, focusing on how modern systems integrate reactive control with deliberative planning to form hybrid architectures. It explains the strengths and weaknesses of each approach and presents the subsumption architecture as a classic example of a reactive, finite‑state‑machine based framework. | Key concepts: Software architecture, Reactive control, Deliberative (model‑based) planning, Hybrid architecture, Subsumption architecture, Finite state machine, Sensor‑driven decision making, Global vs. local control | Example questions: What is the difference between reactive control and deliberative planning in robotic software architectures?; How does the subsumption architecture implement reactive behavior using finite state machines?

children.title: 25.8 Application Domains
children.abstract: This section outlines the primary application domains for robotic technology, illustrating how a pipeline architecture—comprising perception, planning & control, and vehicle interface layers—enables robots to operate concurrently and robustly in settings such as hospitals, fulfillment centers, industry, and agriculture. | Key concepts: Pipeline architecture, Perception layer, Planning and control layer, Vehicle interface layer, Cross‑cutting communication modules, Helpmate robot, Kiva robots, Material‑handling systems, Industrial automation (assembly line, welding, painting), Agricultural/earth‑moving robots | Example questions: What are the main layers of a robot’s pipeline architecture and how do they interact?; In which real‑world domains are robots like Helpmate and Kiva most commonly deployed?

children.title: 25.9 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: This section provides a concise overview of robotics fundamentals, covering robot hardware (sensors, effectors, manipulators, mobile platforms), perception techniques (including probabilistic filtering like Kalman and particle filters), and motion planning in configuration space, as well as brief mentions of teleoperation and humanoid robots. | Key concepts: Sensors and effectors, Manipulator vs. mobile robot, Robotic perception, Kalman filter, Particle filter, Belief state, Configuration space (C‑space), Teleoperation (master–slave configuration), Humanoid robot | Example questions: What are the main types of probabilistic filters used for robot perception and how do they maintain a belief state?; How does motion planning for robots differ when performed in configuration space versus physical workspace?

chapters.title: VII: Conclusions
chapters.abstract: This section explores the philosophical foundations of artificial intelligence, contrasting the weak AI hypothesis (machines can simulate intelligence) with the strong AI hypothesis (machines can truly think). It also discusses how AI is defined in terms of agent programs and highlights the ethical responsibilities of AI researchers. | Key concepts: Weak AI hypothesis, Strong AI hypothesis, Artificial intelligence (AI) definition, Agent program, Digital architecture, Philosophical foundations of AI, Ethical implications of intelligent machines, Computationalism, Simulation vs. real intelligence | Example questions: What is the difference between weak AI and strong AI, and why does it matter for AI research?; How does the textbook define AI in terms of agent programs and digital architectures?

children.title: 26 Philosophical Foundations
children.abstract: This section introduces the philosophical debate surrounding artificial intelligence, distinguishing between the weak AI hypothesis (machines can simulate intelligence) and the strong AI hypothesis (machines can truly think). It also touches on how AI is defined in engineering terms and emphasizes the ethical responsibilities of AI researchers. | Key concepts: Weak AI hypothesis, Strong AI hypothesis, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Computationalism, Agent program, Digital architecture, Simulation vs. real intelligence, Consciousness, Ethical implications of AI | Example questions: What is the difference between weak AI and strong AI, and why does it matter for AI research?; How does the engineering definition of AI as the search for the best agent program relate to the philosophical claims about machine consciousness?

children.title: 26.1 Weak AI: Can Machines Act Intelligently?
children.abstract: This section introduces the philosophical foundations of artificial intelligence, distinguishing between the weak AI hypothesis (machines can simulate intelligence) and the strong AI hypothesis (machines can truly think). It discusses the historical origins of AI, the definition of AI as the search for the best agent program on a given architecture, and highlights the ethical considerations surrounding intelligent machines. | Key concepts: Weak AI hypothesis, Strong AI hypothesis, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Simulation vs. real intelligence, Agent program, Digital architecture, Computationalism, 1956 Dartmouth workshop, Ethical implications of intelligent machines, Enumeration of possible programs | Example questions: What is the difference between weak AI and strong AI, and why do most AI researchers focus on weak AI?; How does the definition of AI as the search for the best agent program on a digital architecture support the possibility of weak AI?

children.title: 26.2 Strong AI: Can Machines Really Think?
children.abstract: This section examines the philosophical challenges to Strong AI, focusing on objections that a machine passing the Turing Test would still lack genuine consciousness, emotions, and intentionality. It discusses Turing’s response, the role of phenomenology, and the embodied cognition perspective that cognition cannot be separated from a body interacting with its environment. | Key concepts: Strong AI, Turing Test, Argument from consciousness, Phenomenology, Intentionality, Embodied cognition, Geoffrey Jefferson objection, Simulation vs. genuine thinking, Mental states in machines | Example questions: What are the main philosophical objections to claiming that a machine can truly think?; How does the embodied cognition approach influence the debate over Strong AI and the Turing Test?

children.title: 26.3 The Ethics and Risks of Developing Artificial Intelligence
children.abstract: This section examines the moral responsibilities of AI researchers by weighing the potential negative and positive impacts of artificial intelligence. It outlines specific ethical concerns—including job displacement, loss of accountability, and existential risk—and argues that engineers must consider whether AI should be pursued at all. | Key concepts: AI ethics, Automation and job displacement, Unintended negative side effects, Loss of accountability, Existential risk of AI, Leisure time imbalance, Human uniqueness, Misuse of AI systems, Moral responsibility of engineers | Example questions: What are the primary ethical risks associated with developing artificial intelligence?; How can AI-driven automation affect employment and what responsibilities do engineers have in addressing this?

children.title: 26.4 Summary, Bibliographical and Historical Notes, Exercises
children.abstract: Section 26.4 reviews the philosophical foundations of AI, contrasting weak and strong AI, summarizing Turing’s behavioral test, and noting the ongoing debate about consciousness, mental states, and potential societal threats. It also touches on historical analogies (e.g., the Odyssey) and the ethical considerations of robot rights. | Key concepts: Weak AI, Strong AI, Turing Test, Mental states as brain states, Consciousness, AI safety / safeguards, Robot rights, Philosophical foundations of AI, Potential societal threats | Example questions: What is the difference between weak AI and strong AI as described in this section?; How does the section relate the story of Ulysses and the sirens to modern AI safety concerns?

children.title: 27 AI: The Present and Future
children.abstract: This section evaluates whether recent advances in AI components and architectures are sufficient to create a general‑purpose intelligent agent. It reviews the utility‑based agent design, its learning component, and questions the adequacy of the rational‑agent paradigm and its broader implications. | Key concepts: Rational agent, Utility function, Percept history, Agent architecture, Learning component, Deliberative (knowledge‑based) agent, Decision‑theoretic agent, General‑purpose intelligent agent, AI progress (scientific and technological), Design goal assessment | Example questions: What criteria does the textbook use to judge if current AI components can lead to a general‑purpose intelligent agent?; How does the utility‑based agent with a learning component illustrate the most general AI design discussed in the chapter?

children.title: 27.1 Agent Components
children.abstract: Section 27.1 reviews the building blocks of intelligent agents, concentrating on the utility‑based agent model and its learning component. It evaluates which components (percepts, actions, utility functions, reasoning methods, representations) are well understood and which gaps remain for creating a general‑purpose intelligent system. | Key concepts: Rational agent, Utility function, Percept history, Reflex agent, Deliberative (knowledge‑based) agent, Decision‑theoretic agent, Learning component, State representation (atomic, factored, structured), Logical reasoning, Probabilistic reasoning | Example questions: What are the main components of a utility‑based agent and how does the learning module fit in?; Which aspects of agent design are still missing for achieving a general‑purpose intelligent agent?

children.title: 27.2 Agent Architectures
children.abstract: This section discusses the need for hybrid agent architectures that combine fast reflexive responses with slower knowledge‑based deliberation, emphasizing that the boundaries between components must be flexible. It also highlights challenges in learning structured, hierarchical representations (e.g., deep belief networks) and the difficulty of building large commonsense knowledge bases, suggesting the Web as a potential source of organized knowledge. | Key concepts: Hybrid agent architecture, Reflex responses, Knowledge‑based deliberation, Deep belief networks, Structured/hierarchical representations, Inductive logic programming, Probabilistic languages, Commonsense knowledge bases, Web as a knowledge source | Example questions: Why do modern AI agents need both reflexive and deliberative components, and how are hybrid architectures designed to support this?; What are the main challenges in using machine learning to acquire structured, hierarchical knowledge for agents, and how might the Web help?

children.title: 27.3 Are We Going in the Right Direction?
children.abstract: The section reflects on the ultimate direction of AI research, questioning whether current progress resembles a modest tree‑climb or a bold rocket journey. It revisits AI’s core goal of building rational agents and contrasts two specifications—perfect rationality and calculative rationality—highlighting their practical limitations. | Key concepts: Perfect rationality, Calculative rationality, Expected utility, Rational agent, Computational feasibility, Decision‑theoretic agents, AI research direction, Dreyfus tree‑climb analogy | Example questions: What is the difference between perfect rationality and calculative rationality in AI?; Does the textbook suggest that aiming for perfect rationality is realistic for building intelligent agents?

children.title: 27.4 What If AI Does Succeed?
children.abstract: Section 27.4 explores the hypothetical scenario in which artificial intelligence achieves its ambitious goals, discussing the ethical responsibilities of AI researchers and the societal impact of varying levels of AI success. It contrasts modest, medium‑level AI achievements—already reshaping education, software development, and everyday applications—with the broader, yet‑to‑be‑realized consequences of truly successful AI. | Key concepts: Bounded optimality, AI success scenarios, Ethical responsibility in AI, Medium‑level AI impacts, AI applications (speech recognition, surveillance, robots, search engines), Pervasive societal effects, David Lodge’s Small World analogy | Example questions: What ethical considerations does the author raise if AI research ultimately succeeds?; How might medium‑level successes in AI change everyday life compared to current technologies like the Internet?

chapters.title: A: Mathematical background
chapters.abstract: This section introduces the mathematical foundations for evaluating algorithm performance, contrasting empirical benchmarking with theoretical analysis. It explains asymptotic analysis, the use of O‑notation, and how to abstract input size and operation counts to estimate time (and memory) complexity. | Key concepts: Benchmarking, Algorithm analysis, Asymptotic analysis, O‑notation, Input size (n), Time complexity, Space complexity, Operation count, Abstract machine model | Example questions: What is the difference between benchmarking an algorithm and performing a mathematical analysis of its complexity?; How can I use asymptotic analysis to determine the O‑notation for a simple summation routine?

children.title: A.1 Complexity Analysis and O() Notation
children.abstract: This section introduces the need for algorithmic complexity analysis, contrasting empirical benchmarking with mathematical, implementation‑independent analysis. It explains how to abstract input size and operation counts, leading to asymptotic analysis and the use of O‑notation to describe algorithm performance. | Key concepts: Benchmarking, Algorithm analysis, Input size (n), Operation count, Asymptotic analysis, Big‑O notation, Implementation independence, Time complexity, Space complexity | Example questions: Why do we use Big‑O notation instead of just measuring runtime on a specific machine?; How do I determine the input parameter n and count operations for a simple summation algorithm?

children.title: A.2 Vectors, Matrices, and Linear Algebra
children.abstract: This section introduces fundamental complexity classes—P, NP, co‑NP, and #P—explaining their relationships, the notion of NP‑complete and co‑NP‑complete problems, and the distinction between decision and counting problems. It also touches on the practical relevance of these classes, using SAT and algorithms like WalkSAT as examples. | Key concepts: P (Polynomial time), NP (Nondeterministic Polynomial time), NP‑complete, co‑NP, co‑NP‑complete, #P (Sharp‑P), Decision problems vs. counting problems, Satisfiability (SAT), WalkSAT algorithm | Example questions: What makes a problem NP‑complete and why is it considered the hardest in NP?; How does the class #P differ from NP, and what type of problems does it capture?
